@@133992863 <p> The world 's largest compressed air energy storage facility has reached full operation in underground salt caverns in the eastern Chinese province of Jiangsu . <p> The Guoxin Suyan Huai'an Salt Cavern Compressed Air Energy Storage Power Generation Project has an installed power output of 600 megawatts(MW) and a storage capacity of 2.4 gigawatt-hours ( GWh ) , or four hours of energy storage duration . <p> The project , which comprises two 300 MW non-combustion compressed air energy storage units , works by compressing air and injecting it into the salt caverns during periods of low demand . The stored air is then released during peak demand to drive turbines and generate electricity . <p> According to Harbin Electric Corporation , which supplied the heat exchange equipment for the project , the facility uses molten salt and pressurised thermal water storage for heat management and has a conversion efficiency of 71 per cent . <p> China 's National Energy Administration announced last week that the two units had been successfully connected to the grid for the first time and simultaneously were able to achieve full-load power generation . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( GW ) of electricity each year , the equivalent of power for 600,000 households , and capable of reducing coal consumption by as much as 250,000 tonnes and carbon dioxide emissions by 600,000 tonnes per year . <p> The NEA says the project represents a new generation of grid " stabiliser , " acting as a buffer between generation and consumption while also improving the sustainability of the region 's electricity grid . <p> Globally , a range of compressed air energy storage ( CAES ) projects are under development in a number of countries , including China , the US , Canada and Europe . <p> In Australia , the 200 MW , up to eight hour ( 1600 MWh ) duration Silver City Energy Storage project is being developed by Canadian compressed air technology company Hydrostor , as part of a world-first renewable energy mini-grid in Broken Hill , New South Wales . <p> Hydrostor already has a successful utility scale facility commercially contracted to the Independent Electricity System Operator ( IESO ) located in Goderich , Ontario , as well as a second project under late-stage @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Hill is a Melbourne-based journalist who has been writing about climate change , clean technology , and electric vehicles for over 15 years . @@134065291 <p> While the government 's Future Made in Australia Act is framed as an economic security initiative , its largest funding commitments are directed toward carbon abatement rather than the preservation of broad-based industrial capability . <p> This imbalance becomes clear when considering gallium , now listed as a priority mineral for Australia 's critical minerals strategic reserve . Gallium can not be produced without bauxite refining , yet Australia 's refining sector is under growing strain . <p> An economic security strategy that is underweight on foundational industries while overweight on downstream or speculative green technologies risks undermining the security it aims to advance . <p> The Future Made in Australia Act ( the Act ) -- the federal government 's primary policy tool for responding to international economic risk -- is set to fund Australia 's new mineral reserve . The selected minerals are crucial for Australia 's and its partners ' defence supply-chain security in the face of Beijing 's persistent weaponisation of control over mineral supply chains . But the list raises a critical point concerning reciprocal linkages between broad-based industrial capacity and niche activities , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the Act are designed . <p> Gallium -- a key input for semiconductors , military-grade radars and a raft of other high-tech goods -- does n't naturally occur as a free element . Rather , it can only be viably sourced through bauxite smelting , during which it accumulates in the caustic liquor by-product . As a result , without a bauxite refining industry , there can be no gallium and no reserve . <p> Gallium production highlights the relationship between a country 's industrial commons , foundational industrial activities and economic complexity . Foundational industrial activities are the backbone of process knowledge , skilled labour , tacit know-how and ultimately a broad industrial capability set that can pivot towards new adjacent industrial activities . In an era of economic insecurity , the ability to expand Australia 's capability set must be the priority goal of the Act . <p> An expanding or stable set of foundational industries allows for proliferation and thickening of a host of upstream and downstream ancillary supply chains in a virtuous cycle of interdependent development . When the process goes into reverse , for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ making economic security policy ever more challenging . Australia 's economy has experienced such atrophy in recent decades , leaving the country with one of the lowest ratings for economic complexity globally , ranking 105th out of 145 countries . <p> The 2024 collapse of Qenos is illustrative . As Australia 's last producer of polyethylene and industrial-use helium , Qenos enabled domestic downstream activities that required engineered plastic , insulation , packaging and specialty polymers . Its closure reduced Australia 's overall capability set and directly led to the closure of chemicals major Indorama 's Sydney complex which , in turn , had lost its only domestic supplier of ethylene . This episode highlighted the compounding atrophy effects of deindustrialisation . <p> Australia 's metal refining sector is similarly struggling under high energy costs . Traditionally , economists decry efforts at bailing out so-called legacy industries . On a narrow economising level , that is reasonable , but economists ' models assume a benign international market that will always supply goods if the price is paid . That assumption is no longer the baseline for a geoeconomic world facing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of foundational industrial activities must involve a revised cost-benefit calculation that internalises national economic security effects . <p> These insights should inform the resourcing of the Act 's two core work streams : the net zero transformation stream ; and the economic security and resilience stream . Currently , the two largest outlays of the Act are the A$6.7 billion Hydrogen Production Tax Incentive in the net zero stream and the A$7 billion Critical Minerals Production Tax Incentive in the economic resilience stream . Green hydrogen is receiving a tax incentive value similar to that which is available to 31 critical minerals , indicating that the Act 's current priority is reducing emissions rather than improving economic security overall . <p> But the green hydrogen bet was always a gamble for Australia , given the high shipping costs and low export demand . Investors are pulling back from the sector as this reality bites . The federal government should follow suit . The billion-dollar ' solar sunshot ' plan for building solar panels is equally speculative . Australia 's chances to succeed where Europe 's and the United States ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The Act over-privileges the green transition workstream at the expense of broader strategic economic resilience . It should re-focus on explicit prioritisation of sectors that deliver maximum economic security , including key defence sector inputs , rather than maximum emissions reduction . Canberra should focus on building out foundational industries where Australia has existing comparative advantages that can be leveraged for development of the country 's industrial capability set . <p> While Australia 's ability to influence global climate change through policies under the Act is negligible , the government 's ability to influence the nation 's geoeconomic security is vast . The economic resilience workstream should be the Act 's priority stream . <p> Author <p> Naoise McDonagh is Senior Lecturer and MBA Director at ECU 's School of Business and Law .

@@134065335 <h> When America raises the bill , Australia pays the price <p> As Washington demands unprecedented military spending from its allies , Australia faces a stark choice between strategic loyalty and the preservation of its social and economic foundations , writes Imran Khalid . <p> IN THE SWEEPING architecture of the 2026 National Defence Strategy , Washington has issued a decree that is as fiscally daunting as it is strategically blunt . <p> For decades , the United States has acted as the venture capitalist of global security , providing the lion 's share of the " seed funding " for regional stability , while its allies have contributed niche capabilities . But under the new doctrine of ' Restoring Peace Through Strength ' , the terms of the lease have changed . Nowhere is the " sticker shock " more profound than in Canberra . <p> The 2026 NDS introduces a new gold standard for what it calls ' model allies ' : a requirement to spend 3.5% of GDP on core military capabilities and an additional 1.5% on security-related expenses . For Australia , currently hovering at roughly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ adjustment ; it is a fundamental reordering of the Australian social contract . <p> To understand the magnitude of this shift , one must look at the numbers . Reaching a total of 5% of GDP would require Australia to nearly double its defence outlays -- an additional $40 billion annually -- at a time when the domestic economy is grappling with the familiar headwinds of the 21st Century : an ageing population , a strained healthcare system and the expensive transition to a green economy . <p> If Canberra were to meet this American benchmark , the defence budget would begin to rival the entire federal spend on education or health . It raises a haunting question : Can a nation be truly secure if its strategic weight comes at the expense of its internal resilience ? <p> The tragedy of the current moment is that Australia has already been doing the heavy lifting . Through the AUKUS agreement , Canberra has committed to a multi-decade path to acquiring nuclear-powered submarines -- the most ambitious industrial undertaking in the nation 's history . Yet , in the eyes of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ special exemption ; it is simply the baseline . <p> The Biden-era concept of " integrated deterrence " has been replaced by a more transactional " offshore balancing " . Washington is effectively saying that while it will provide the " Golden Dome " of missile defence and the high-end nuclear umbrella , the " boots on the ground " in the First Island Chain must increasingly bear a local flag . <p> This " America First " realism was personified by the 3 January capture of Venezuelan President Nicol ? s Maduro during Operation Absolute Resolve . By acting unilaterally to secure the Western Hemisphere , Washington has signalled that its focus has shifted toward homefront stability and direct resource control . <p> For Australia , this provides a chilling preview : the U.S. is increasingly unwilling to subsidise the security of distant " secondary " theatres unless those allies are fully " staked " into the new Board of Peace financial architecture . <p> For Australian policymakers , the challenge is twofold . First , there is the " guns vs butter " dilemma . In a vibrant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ national wealth on long-range missiles when voters are feeling the pinch of housing and energy prices . Second , there is the risk of " strategic over-extension " . By tailoring its entire force structure to meet American requirements for a " denial defence " against China , Australia risks losing the flexibility to manage its own " near abroad " in the South Pacific -- where threats are often about climate change and state fragility rather than kinetic conflict . <p> Furthermore , this pivot ignores the reality that a fragile domestic economy is itself a national security vulnerability . If the Australian Government cannibalises its Social Services and Medicare funding to purchase Tomahawk missiles , it risks radicalising a disillusioned youth and fracturing the social cohesion that underpins national mobilisation . The 2026 NDS treats allies like satellite offices in a corporate restructuring , but a nation is not a subsidiary . <p> When the " cost of doing business " with Washington becomes synonymous with the erosion of the Australian way of life , the alliance ceases to be a shield and begins to feel like a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inadvertently push Australia toward a more independent " armed neutrality " style of thinking . We are seeing the early signs of this in the Albanese Government 's attempt to " re-label " spending on cyber resilience and critical minerals as " security-related " to bridge the gap toward that 5% target . It is a clever bit of accounting , but it does not solve the underlying tension . <p> The United States must be careful . By treating its most loyal allies as franchises that must pay a high royalty fee , it risks hollowing out the very goodwill that makes the alliance system a unique American advantage . <p> For Australia , the path forward requires a delicate balance . True strength does not come from a spreadsheet alone . If the 2026 NDS forces Australia into a choice between its alliance and its domestic prosperity , the result may be a fortress that is impressively armed , but socially and economically brittle . In the long run , that is a recipe for a weaker Indo-Pacific , not a stronger one . <p> Imran Khalid is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ work has been widely published by prestigious international news organisations . <h> Save IA <p> It 's never been more important to help Independent Australia survive ! <p> Fearless news publication IA has exposed deep-rooted secrets other media routinely ignored . @@134065337 <h> Naming the real problem with our climate <p> Our climate is collapsing because our comfort depends on systems that exploit people and nature elsewhere , writes Mark Beeson . <p> ONE REASON WHY so many of us are concerned about climate change is because we know what we mean when we say it . True , there is still a surprisingly large group of people who do n't believe it 's happening , think it 's overstated or could n't give a toss either way , but we can at least agree what we 're referring to . <p> It 's not possible to try and address a problem unless we can identify it and convince other people that it 's worth thinking about , even if we come to different conclusions about what , if anything , should be done . Plenty of people are currently experiencing the " housing crisis " , for example , but it helps to label it , if only so undeservedly affluent boomers like me recognise that there 's a problem . <p> Here 's a phrase you probably have n't come @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its rather nerdy , academic sound : the imperial mode of living . As a rather nerdy ( ex ) academic myself , that 's the sort of thing I would like , no doubt , but it merits five minutes of your time , and possibly a lot more . <p> Originally coined by two German scholars , the imperial mode of living is a shorthand way of describing ' a set of production and consumption patterns that are , by and large , based on the premise that there is an unlimited availability of nature and labour power at a global scale . ' <p> Not only are Brand and Wissen also nerdy academics , but they 're Marxists , too . That 's another label that carries a lot of baggage , but the basic point is that endless economic growth on a finite planet is not just impossible , but it involves the Global North exploiting the Global South in environmentally unsustainable and morally indefensible ways . <p> So far , so Marxy , perhaps , but that 's not the end of the potentially bad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , capitalists or intimate cronies of U.S. President Donald Trump are partly to blame for this unfortunate and exploitative state of affairs , I 'm afraid . <p> Even in a supposedly post-colonial era , the basic global division of labour still involves extracting resources , including labour , from the ' developing world ' , a process that benefits workers in the North at the expense of their counterparts in the South . <p> There are clear limits to this idea , but it captures something important . It 's true that some resource-based economies , like Australia , have done rather well out of the globalisation of production processes that rely on material inputs like iron ore , gas and coal . But we are an exception that proves a more general rule about the " resource curse " and the creation of parasitic elites and mass exploitation . <p> One of Brand and Wissen 's key claims is that the well-being of wage-earners in the North is dependent on ' the smooth functioning of precisely those production structures and infrastructures whose resource and emissions intensity is increasingly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . ' In other words , everyone in the North , not just the super-rich , are complicit in the immiseration of the South , albeit to ( much ) greater or lesser degrees . <p> My intention is not to make readers feel guilty about their comparatively gilded lifestyles , but to recognise how atypical and possibly unsustainable they are . Some forms of conspicuous consumption really do stand out in this regard . Another noteworthy neologism that 's unlikely to catch on in this country is ' petro-masculinity ' , but it strikes a chord too . <p> In a more innocent and ill-informed era we might have indulged the self-absorbed actions of rev-heads , but anyone who drives around in a small(ish) truck called a ' Raptor ' at this pivotal historical juncture looks ripe for some well-intentioned criticism . <p> To be fair , it 's hard to understand complex economic and social relationships that span continents and threaten the future of the planet . But if monstrous SUV owners ca n't refrain from endangering fellow road users and pedestrians , they are n't likely to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about . <p> We might hope that some enlightened leadership and an informed , open-ended national debate about the increasingly visible climate crisis , its causes and our individual and collective role in its intensification , could encourage a sense of social responsibility . But our government does n't seem to care about the environment , so why should we ? <p> Indeed , to judge by the actions of politicians like Scott Morrison , who claimed that **25;229;TOOLONG types were trying to ' end the weekend ' and undermine the Australian way of life , ' responsible politician ' is becoming an oxymoron . Morrison may be uniquely unprincipled in Australian political history , but he knew how to touch a nerve . <p> Dispiriting ? For sure . Environmental Design in 1995 . <p> He quickly established himself in the profession , working with the prestigious Sydney firm Leighton Irwin before embarking on travels through Europe to broaden his understanding of architectural styles . <p> Ross 's career trajectory soon took him to architectural offices in Sydney and London , where he won a number of design competitions . <p> His talent and @@134139563 <p> Federal Labor has launched a major review of the " governance arrangements " of the Australian Energy Market Operator , nearly 17 years after the independent body was first established to manage the nation 's rapidly evolving electricity and gas markets . <p> Federal energy minister Chris Bowen announced the review of AEMO on Friday , after it was agreed to at the latest Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council ( ECMC ) meeting in December . <p> Bowen says the review , to be led by senior governance expert Nigel Ray , aims to ensure that AEMO remains " fit for purpose " as Australia 's national electricity grid transitions to 82 per cent renewables by 2030 and net zero by 2050 . <p> AEMO was originally established in 2009 to manage the day-today operation and administration of both the power system and electricity wholesale spot market in the NEM , the retail electricity markets , the retail and wholesale gas markets and planning and development of transmission . <p> Since 2018 , AEMO also has been charged with publishing a regularly updated Integrated System Plan ( ISP @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ National Electricity Market to supply affordable and reliable electricity while transitioning to net zero . The ISP was itself the subject of a review launched in 2024 . <p> Further , the market operator 's responsibilities have bloated out to include governing grid system strength , reliability and reserve trading ; gas market reliability and security ; market and system advisory and analysis services , and ; services to jurisdictional energy investment schemes . <p> As Renew Economy has reported , AEMO has argued since the release of the very first editions of the ISP -- under the then Coalition government -- that renewables and storage offer the lowest cost and most reliable replacement for the country 's ageing coal fired power stations . <p> Its modelling and planning blueprint were largely ignored by the Coalition government which , since being relegated to Opposition benches , has used AEMO as something of a punching bag in its push for nuclear and baseload . @@134139583 <p> A new analysis of the European Union 's decision to weaken CO2 emissions standards for cars by replacing its original 2035 zero-emissions target with a 90 per cent reduction will introduce high levels of uncertainty that could see battery electric vehicle ( BEV ) sales slip by as much as 50 per cent . <p> While the Commission claimed that its revisions were " ambitious " and designed to " ensure 2050 climate neutrality and strategic independence " , the fact that they no longer call for a complete phaseout of internal combustion engines mean that they are a downgrade on previous legislation under the guise of being " pragmatic policy ... while providing more flexibility to manufacturers . @@134171422 <h> The sovereign citizen ' workshops ' clogging up Australian courts <p> David Heilpern was going undercover . A New South Wales magistrate for 22 years , and now dean of law at Southern Cross University , he wore a flannelette shirt and broad-brimmed hat to better disguise himself . His quarry was a notorious pseudo-law " guru " , a man who travels the country giving paid workshops to people desperate to avoid various legal consequences -- often traffic infringements or asset seizures . <p> The man is not a lawyer . He is not licensed to dispense legal advice , and his website -- where he solicits membership fees for his " club " -- is filled with suspiciously verbose disclaimers regarding his liability . Nonetheless , he receives money for spouting arcane " gobbledegook " to credulous audiences . " The number of these profiteers is increasing , " Heilpern tells The Saturday Paper . " And they are performing to full audiences . They offer subscription-based services and they claim to have tens of thousands of members . But their sales pitch is : ' it works ' . It 's not just obtuse but fraudulent . They tout successes that do n't exist . " <p> This is the strange world of sovereign citizens , pseudo-law and the profiteers who offer bizarre , vexatious and fatally flawed legal advice to the aggrieved and desperate . The strong anecdotal evidence from magistrates across the country is that " warfare by paper " , and the prevalence of hostile sovereign citizens representing themselves in courts , is quickly increasing and placing enormous pressure on an already strained judicial system . <p> Grasping the logic of sovereign citizens is much like wrestling a column of smoke , but at its most basic it 's a selective rejection of state authority , which is often described as both tyrannical and legally baseless . Sovereign citizens will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ straw man " and their real , flesh-and-blood self . The straw man is a legal construct -- it 's often likened to a corporate identity -- that the state imposes on individuals at birth . In their peculiar attempts to squirm free of this authority , sovereign citizens will invoke their flesh-and-blood selves as distinct from and superior to the supposed straw man . <p> Clear ? If not , do n't worry ; it 's often not clear to magistrates . " There was great uncertainty . People feared @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ And pseudo-law popped up again as an idea : well , actually , you do n't need to pay a mortgage . It 's all fake anyway . And we saw at this point gurus who make money selling these schemes started travelling from the United States , travelling to Australia , travelling elsewhere to kind of seed it and to find consumers who are willing to pay for this stuff . " <p> Hobbs says the Covid crisis and the resulting conspicuous exercise of state authority regarding lockdowns and vaccination supercharged the popularity of the idea . " Covid was another structural crisis and it exploded in popularity again . @@134171428 <h> Elliot Stein The politics of palliative care <p> I 've had the privileged heartbreak of being with two loved ones at the end of their lives . <p> When my father died a little over five years ago , it was in a dedicated palliative care ward in a regional private hospital . Pain management and end-of-life treatment was the core of his care plan in those final weeks . <p> The volumes and mixtures of pain medications were confronting . The doctor reassured us . " Do n't worry , " they said . " Good pain relief does n't kill people , cancer kills people . When he sleeps , he 'll be thinking of his happiest place . " We nodded , cried and thought of the beach . <p> I learnt that palliative care gives dignity and quality in place of pain . <p> When my 99-year-old grandmother died in the early days of January this year , it was in an aged-care home in Sydney 's north at the end of a nine-month stay . The experience could not have been more different . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in that setting palliative care was a rare exception . Only after a family-initiated intervention by an external NSW Health service was palliative relief provided . <p> When you enter an aged-care home , you discuss an advanced care plan , giving instructions about care during a life-ending moment -- for instance , whether or not you wish to be resuscitated -- but for the months leading up to that moment , there 's no equivalent palliative care plan to make informed decisions on how to treat and manage symptoms and pain . <p> Despite the findings of a royal commission and the great strides of the new Aged Care Act , quality palliative care inside aged-care homes still feels hopelessly out of reach to too many . Dignity is lost to those who pass without a voice . <p> In the weeks since my grandmother 's death , as I 've sought to turn grief into something meaningful , I 've been wondering what was missing from our system -- a system that I had the unique opportunity to influence over the years , and one I thought I @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ professional expertise in the sector to get basic palliative care to an aged-care resident . If death is the one true certainty , why is it so hard to get the right support ? Why have n't I thought more about it before ? Why have n't we all done more ? <p> As I 've shared my own story I 've heard more from friends , neighbours and professionals about how their family members died , what treatment was and was n't given , how they navigated the system . <p> I 've realised that my grandmother 's case was n't unusual at all . Too much of the end-of-life experience remains under a veil -- felt sharply then forgotten . Fixing the system begins by ending the syndrome of death denial in Australia . Too often we hide behind cosy euphemisms that mask the realities of the end of life , when speaking plainly means we can improve things for all . <p> One palliative doctor in Melbourne told me that good end-of-life care is like " playing all the keys on the piano " , providing holistic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of treatments , pain relief , comfort , conversation , spiritual and social interaction . <p> There are caring , qualified and exceptional staff inside aged-care homes across the country , but the numbers of Australians dying without much-needed palliative care tells the story of how disjointed the system has become . <p> Three in five patients who die from terminal illness in Australia receive no specialist palliative care , and about half of all deaths of people aged over 85 occur in aged-care homes . <p> In 2021 the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety found a high standard of palliative care " should be considered core business " of residential aged care . It said that staff are often under-educated on this service . A Palliative Care Australia workforce survey reported that half of all aged-care staff believe palliative delivery stagnated or decreased in 2024 . <p> The average length of stay in residential aged-care homes is getting shorter . In Brisbane I met an elderly lady who had lived in an aged-care home for 20 years . Today she would be an extreme outlier , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It feels crass to say people enter residential aged care to die , but of the nearly 300,000 Australians who enter aged care each year , the overwhelming majority do so over the age of 85 , when their clinical and care needs are acute , requiring increasing levels of support . <p> For years I 've been giving a throwaway line in policy circles , that the future of the residential aged-care business model would morph into " fancy palliative " . I did n't fully appreciate what that meant and how far away it remains . <p> First , amid the gloom , some good news : since the new Aged Care Act took effect in November last year , every Australian has the legal right to equitable access to palliative and end-of-life care . It 's in the law , it 's in the regulations and the funding exists . <p> We now find ourselves in that murky netherworld between reform and implementation , when the excitement of a big vote in parliament has passed and all that is left is the grind of the necessary real-world @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but without training and practices embedded into the more than 2600 aged-care homes in Australia , it 's all a matter of time and chance . A palliative assessment must occur as part of the aged-care admission process , with services explained and provided . <p> Until this work is complete , families are in a lottery of facilities and shifts . One worker in a home might be trained , but not all . The morning crew could be proficient in recognising pain symptoms , the evening shift not so . <p> In addition , government and regulators need to track take-up of training closely and release timely data about homes ' access to funding of palliative care . Where it 's low , proactive teams should be visiting and finding out why . <p> Other big challenges remain . Aged-care homes are federally funded and regulated , while palliative support is state regulated and often jointly funded . The systems rarely speak well to each other . Where there are gaps in the provision of care in aged-care homes , residents can be all too easily bounced back @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ranks as the leading cause of death in Australia . You ca n't administer quality palliative care if you ca n't recognise the complex pain symptoms in dementia patients , yet these professions remain largely siloed . <p> The need to train the cohort of visiting GPs adds another layer of complexity . These doctors often hold clinical governance for aged-care residents , with the ability to sign off on treatment plans and prescriptions . <p> These issues do n't begin to address the needs that arise when palliative care is delivered in the recipient 's own home . While such care does reduce the strain on our hospital systems and provides greater dignity for the patient , it is subject to an absurd three-month limit . Funding is effectively restricted if a patient does n't die within 90 days . <p> None of this is exciting , but it is the reality of policy implementation . <p> Camilla Rowland is embarking on that work already . Palliative care must be the norm for people experiencing end-of-life illness . <p> Families crave certainty . They expect that someone , anyone , will arrive and tell them what to do . @@134171431 <h> John Hewson What Albanese could learn from Mark Carney <p> Without doubt , the most disturbing aspect of today 's geopolitical scene is the paucity of global leadership . United States President Donald Trump continues to undermine a host of multilateral institutions and upend established alliances and agreements as he pursues his imperialist agenda , igniting conflicts along the way . <p> While world leaders such as France 's Emmanuel Macron , the United Kingdom 's Keir Starmer and Germany 's Friedrich Merz have occasionally taken strong positions on specific issues , the stand-out has been Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney . He represents what he unequivocally describes as a " middle power " , one seeking to divest itself from reliance on a major power and potentially set an example for the rest of the world . With his bold statements at the World Economic Forum in Davos , Switzerland , last month , Carney has built on his important 2025 speech in response to Trump 's imposition of punitive tariffs on Canadian exports to the US . <p> Davos is often derided these days as a talkfest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for calling out what so many have been avoiding . He delivered a clear warning and call to action to his audience of government and business leaders , backed by strong intellectual and policy credentials . The speech was all the more remarkable coming from a former central banker -- Carney led the Bank of Canada during the global financial crisis , and the Bank of England after that -- a role not exactly known for straight talking . <p> " Today I will talk about a rupture in the world order , the end of a pleasant fiction and the beginning of a harsh reality , " Carney said . " It seems that every day we 're reminded that we live in an era of great power rivalry , that the rules-based order is fading , that the strong can do what they can , and the weak must suffer what they must ... We are in the midst of a rupture , not a transition , " he warned . <p> " You can not live within the lie of mutual benefit through integration , when integration @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some respects , Albanese was already ahead of his Canadian counterpart 's wake-up call ... What remains now is to clearly establish a productive working relationship with Carney , to develop effective middle power coalitions . <p> The " fiction " that has prevailed in international relations since World War II , and on which countries such as Australia have relied , is that we are all protected under a rules-based international order , strengthened by institutions such as the United Nations , the World Trade Organization , the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the World Health Organization . <p> Carney exposes the lie by invoking late Czech intellectual V ? clav Havel in his essay " The Power of the Powerless " , which explains that the communist system 's power did n't come from the truth but from everyone 's willingness to perform as if it were true . The fragility of the system also stems from this -- when even just one person stops performing , the illusion cracks . <p> The cleverness of Carney 's speech was that he never mentioned Trump . @@134171436 <h> Trans pioneer Beverly Glenn-Copeland 's new album -- recorded in the wake of his dementia diagnosis -- calls for joy in the face of the inevitable . By Daniel Herborn . <p> In September 2024 , the American-born Canadian musician Beverly Glenn-Copeland revealed in an Instagram video that he had been privately managing dementia . Sitting with his creative partner and wife , Elizabeth Copeland , Glenn-Copeland -- who came out as trans in 2002 and adopted the first name Glenn although he still records as Beverly -- seemed at peace with the news . Given the defiance baked into its @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to his back catalogue , it 's almost unbearably poignant . <p> While the 82-year-old has come to prominence only in the past decade , Glenn-Copeland 's musical career stretches back to the early 1960s , when he was one of the first Black students to study at Montreal 's McGill University . He drew on this classical training and a childhood spent listening to his parents sing Black spirituals and play big band jazz standards on the piano to create a pair of records that also incorporated pastoral folk and science fiction . <p> Those first two albums did n't find an audience and Glenn-Copeland 's musical output ground to a halt as he pursued another career in children 's television . Often living in seclusion , studying Buddhism and practising silence , he was far removed from the passing fads of the music industry , a mindset that allowed him to create the idiosyncratic self-released 1986 cassette Keyboard Fantasies , a celebration of Canada 's natural beauty composed entirely on a Yamaha DX7 digital synthesiser and a Roland TR-707 drum machine . Its meagre sales were reportedly mostly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a curio until its rediscovery in 2015 by a Japanese record collector . Reissued the following year , it became an instant cult classic . There was also a new record , 2023 's The Ones Ahead , which expanded his musical palette even further , incorporating African drumming . Either admired as a Gaelic Achilles or despised as a malevolent goon , Keane himself did a grand job of obscuring the finer grain of his soul by stomping opponents or striking teammates in hotel rooms . <p> Captain of Manchester United from 1997 to 2005 -- a good slice of their golden era -- Keane looked unfavourably upon frivolity . Part of the job , he thought , was to radiate an aura of invincible purpose -- he entered stadiums like boxers enter rings . He was known to lash giggling teammates , and later , as a manager of Sunderland , his combustible temper was provoked by his squad playing ABBA 's " Dancing Queen " in the dressing-room just before a game . <p> He once headbutted his goalkeeper , Peter Schmeichel , in a hotel corridor . His feud with Arsenal 's Patrick Vieira @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ included squeezed throats and malicious tackles . Most notorious , though , was the grievous bodily harm -- one ca n't call it a " tackle " -- he inflicted on Manchester City 's Alf-Inge Haaland in 2001 . <p> Four years earlier , Haaland had made the mistake of accusing Keane -- then writhing on the pitch with a torn ACL -- of faking injury . Keane thought this a profane slander and nursed his grievance for years . In April 2001 , during a Manchester derby , Keane smashed Haaland 's right knee with the studs of his boot . <p> One thing about Roy Keane is that his smouldering temper and sense of furious rectitude can never be doused -- a perpetual flame blazes within his troubled head -- and the next year , in his first autobiography , it was with a reckless honesty that he recounted his assault of Haaland . <p> There may not be a more famous -- or legally consequential -- passage of a footballer 's memoir than this : " I 'd waited almost 180 minutes for Alfie , three years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ had the ball on the far touchline . Alfie was taking the piss . I 'd waited long enough . I fucking hit him hard . The ball was there ( I think ) . Take that , you cunt . And do n't stand over me again sneering about fake injuries . " <p> The Football Association 's eyes widened , and so too Haaland 's : here was Keane seemingly admitting his grievous intent and premeditation . He was called before a tribunal and when Keane 's ghostwriter -- the former Irish international Eamon Dunphy -- testified to his belief that , yes , Keane had intentionally tried to injure Haaland , well , the die was cast : Keane was suspended for five matches and fined ? 150,000 . <p> But no , Roy Keane was not merely a thug . He 's Ireland 's greatest player , a midfielder of sublime vision , passing ability and endurance . The grim , dead-eyed skinhead was just a part of a man who obsessively monitored his own commitment , bravery and loyalty . A man who inspired fear @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ family . A man whose temper was spectacularly flammable and alienating and yet was typically ignited by a consistent set of principles . <p> A man whose anger and unforgiving standards often made him seem very lonely indeed . <p> Never mind the seeming obscurity of its subject , nor the modesty of its gaze -- Saipan is a quietly brilliant sports film rarely interested in the dynamics of a team 's conflicting egos . <p> Unless you 're an Irish soccer fan , the premise of Saipan may strike you as curiously obscure and thin : a dramatisation of the Irish national squad 's pre-World Cup camp in 2002 , and the subsequent conflict between manager Mick McCarthy ( played by Steve Coogan ) and his captain , Roy Keane ( ? anna Hardwicke ) , that devolved so bitterly that Keane returned home just days before the tournament began . <p> Personally , I 'm fond of biopics that linger upon a very narrow timeframe , specific moments that contain a revealing concentration of conflict . One of the best sports films I know of , The Damned @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spent as the doomed manager of Leeds United -- and I can only hope this approach might be applied one day to Steve Waugh 's decision to drop vice-captain Shane Warne on the 1999 Windies tour , or David Boon 's folkloric consumption of beers on a Sydney to London flight 10 years earlier . <p> Irish people of a certain age wo n't soon forget the moment that dominated their news for weeks , which seemed perfectly to cleave the public 's sympathies and was thought so disastrous to their World Cup campaign that the Irish prime minister offered to broker a peace deal between McCarthy and Keane . <p> The Roy Keane of Saipan is not the thug of caricature but the meticulous , combustible and intensely proud man who applies his unforgiving standards for himself with equal ferocity to everyone else . As is true of the flesh-and-blood Keane , we see here a man who , for reasons perhaps not entirely clear to himself , will tolerate no weakness , disloyalty or unearnt levity . And if his teammates might occasionally suffer from his uninhibited tongue @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ both on and off the pitch . <p> His antagonist is his manager Mick McCarthy , English-born to an Irish father and who played for Ireland 57 times , including in the 1990 World Cup -- only their second appearance of three . While Saipan makes no obvious demand that the viewer 's sympathy land exclusively with either man , McCarthy here -- perhaps not helped by some Alan Partridge-like mannerisms from Coogan -- seems slightly hapless and incapable of understanding , much less mollifying , the growing dissatisfaction of his captain . <p> Ireland 's qualification for the 2002 World Cup was a significant achievement and Keane 's performances were central to it . So when he lands on the Pacific Island of Saipan for camp and finds a relatively squalid hotel with broken air-conditioning , " rock hard " and " dangerous " training pitches and a buffet offering grim-looking cheese sandwiches , Keane sees -- as he did when Haaland slandered him in ' 97 -- an insult to his integrity and professionalism . <p> If this might seem like the preening indulgence of a millionaire star @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ seemed to some back in Ireland . But for the Keane of Saipan -- and he 's made this point himself , in real life -- the insult of the camp 's preparation went far beyond his own discomfort . <p> This was a professional side subject to unprofessional conditions , and it insulted not only Keane 's dignity but Ireland 's -- it was unthinkable that the England team would be subject to the same . @@134228377 <p> While many were winding down in the lead up to Christmas , the body which writes our energy regulations -- the Australian Energy Market Commission ( AEMC ) -- proposed a radical change in how households should be charged for electricity . <p> This change would mean that in the majority of cases households would no longer pay electricity network monopolies based on how much power they draw from the network and when they do it . <p> Instead , they would pay a substantially inflated fixed daily charge . This could involve roughly a quadrupling in the network fixed charge , although it will vary from around a 350% increase in some networks ( NSW and QLD networks ) to a 500% increase in others ( Victorian networks ) . <p> So the pensioner in a small cottage home , who makes sure they wear their winter woollies to keep their heating bill down , and always takes short showers and who used their small surplus cash to buy solar to contain their power bill , will be hit with the same bill to use the network as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their pool in winter , never switches their ducted air conditioner off in Summer , and who swears off solar as something for hippies and lefties . <p> For many of you this may seem so ridiculous that it ca n't be true . But according to the AEMC this will be far fairer and more economically efficient than the current network tariff framework . <p> This current tariff framework , by the way , was also the result of an AEMC inquiry recommendation made back in 2012 to introduce what it called , ' cost-reflective tariffs ' . <p> This inquiry ( entitled Power of Choice ) was commissioned in the wake of a 70% increase in power prices over the preceding 4 years driven mainly by electricity networks splurging tens of billions of dollars on expanding their assets . <p> At the time networks justified this huge increase in costs as necessary to cater for what they claimed would be a large increases in electricity demand for household air conditioning . <p> The AEMC recommended that to ensure such large increases in network costs were avoided in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for their usage during periods of high demand for network capacity ( roughly 2pm to 9pm on hot and cold days ) , but with compensating lower prices at other times when network capacity was unconstrained . <p> While this reform would hurt solar owners as well as big users of air conditioning , according to the AEMC back in 2012 , this would be more economically efficient because it would ensure we minimised expenditure on expensive network capacity expansions that were poorly utilised . <p> Plus , it would be fairer because those that got the greatest benefit from use of network capacity would pay the most . <p> This AEMC reform has ultimately led to consumers being compulsorily required to pay for upgrades to smart meters , with solar owners being prioritised as the first to pay . <p> This has been accompanied by network businesses shifting households progressively over to new tariffs that charged more for power during peak demand periods and less in off-peak periods , again with solar owners ( who lost out from this deal ) prioritised to be shifted to these new tariffs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all that . Apparently , we have so much spare network capacity that consumers should stop being so careful about when they use electricity , and be encouraged to use far more . Given networks have spent so much money building lots of network capacity it would be economically wasteful not to use it . <p> Also , according to the AEMC , it would be fairer if everyone paid the same amount to the network irrespective of their need for network capacity , because rich people are installing batteries that reduce their peak demand to almost nothing , meanwhile those who rent ca n't get these systems . <p> So what 's the truth here ? One thing we know for sure is that this new recommendation would be extremely good for the shareholders in electricity distribution networks . <p> Unfortunately for these shareholders , growth in household electricity peak demand has evaporated which has removed the opportunity for growth in their asset base and therefore revenues . As you 'd imagine they 'd really much prefer to see their revenues growing . <p> Also , what company would @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ amount even if that customer 's demand for their production capacity is declining . <p> Especially when it comes with upside that if demand for their service did actually grow , perhaps because of widespread electric vehicle charging during the evening peak period , then they 'll get to grow their revenues . <p> But in terms of fairness the AEMC 's recommendation is like a Robin Hood scheme in reverse . <p> What the boffins in the AEMC do n't seem to realise ( or have perhaps chosen to ignore ? ) is that low income households consume noticeably less electricity than high income households . <p> That has been found from survey after survey from bodies like the Bureau of Statistics , state regulators , and Energy Consumers Australia . This remains true even with the proliferation of solar systems . As an example , the chart below is taken from 2023 survey of energy consumers by Energy Consumers Australia . <p> It clearly shows that as incomes rise so does the energy bill , with high income households paying almost double the energy bill of low income @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ twice as much energy from energy suppliers ( and not from their solar and battery system for which there is no energy bill ) . <p> Therefore , a move to switch away from charging for network services based on power demand to one that was simply fixed per household is that the poor will pay more for electricity and the rich will pay less . <p> Also , it is complete myth that solar and battery adoption is concentrated amongst high income earners . The chart below maps postcodes around Australia in terms of their average household income relative to the level of battery adoption amongst those households under the Federal Government 's Cheaper Home Batteries Program . <p> There is no correlation between income levels within a postcode and the proportion of households adopting batteries . <p> What we know from other studies is that renters are missing out on solar and batteries , but amongst those who have a mortgage or own a home outright , poorer households install solar at a similar or greater rate than richer households . <p> Source : Clean Energy Regulator for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ households by postcode . <p> In lieu of the lack of quantitative analysis by the AEMC ( but geez they 're good at vignettes ) , Green Energy Markets has analysed the impact of a switch to fixed network pricing in terms of equity outcomes ( low income versus high income households ) and also the financial attractiveness of adopting a solar and battery system with its implications for emission reduction goals . " <h> What are sleeper sharks ? <p> Sleeper sharks are large sharks with mottled skin and small fins that dwell in the oceanfrom the surface to thousands of metres deep . <p> Two similar-looking species are believed to live in the southern hemisphere , the Southern sleeper shark and the Pacific sleeper shark ( Somniosus pacificus ) . <p> The Southern sleeper shark was first identified from a sketch of a washed-up specimen on Macquarie Island in 1913 , as part of a scientific mission to Sub-Antarctic islands and the Antarctic led by Sir Douglas Mawson . <p> Not much is known about the species , with most of our knowledge coming from rare collections as fisheries bycatch . <p> New Zealand biologist Harold Hamilton sketched a washed-up sleeper shark on Macquarie Island @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by Sir Douglas Mawson . ( Supplied : Mitchell Library , State Library of New South Wales/Australian Antarctic Division ) <p> Southern sleepers were thought to be limited to the southern hemisphere while Pacific sleepers were restricted to the north Pacific . <p> But it is unclear whether the Southern sleeper shark and Pacific sleeper shark are separate species . @@134264328 <p> Researchers from the University of Sydney say they have created a process that uses liquid metals and sunlight to produce green hydrogen from both freshwater and seawater . <p> Green hydrogen -- hydrogen produced using only renewable sources -- has been the focus of researchers and scientists across the globe looking to decarbonise hard-to-abate sectors like transport , manufacturing , agriculture , and major industry . <p> But even though the process of producing green hydrogen is well known , and predominantly focused on splitting water using methods such as electrolysis , photocatalysis , and plasma ( artificial lightning ) , there are nevertheless a number of obstacles to this method that often lead to high costs or low yields . <p> One is cost , and the competition with batteries for a number of sectors such as passenger vehicles , and the other has been access to fresh water . <p> That 's where the new research from Professor Kourosh Kalantar-Zadeh , from the School of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering , and his team at the University of Sydney come in , having developed a circular process that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " hydrogen molecules from both freshwater and seawater . <p> Gallium is a metal with a low melting point , meaning that it needs less energy to transition from a solid into a liquid . For example , while gallium looks like a solid metal at room temperature , when heated to body temperature it transforms into liquid metallic puddles . <p> Lead author and PhD candidate Luis Campos describes the surface of liquid gallium as very chemically " non-sticky " , with most materials unable to attach to it under normal conditions . <p> But when gallium is suspended in water and exposed to light , the liquid metal reacts at its surface , gradually oxidising and corroding and then creating clean hydrogen and gallium oxyhydroxide on its surface . <p> Importantly , once the hydrogen is extracted , " the gallium oxyhydroxide can also be reduced back into gallium and reused for future hydrogen production -- which we term a circular process , " explained Professor Kalantar-Zadeh . <p> " Gallium has not been explored before as a way to produce hydrogen at high rates when in contact @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ previously . Here are a couple of examples : <p> So : What 's happening ? Has plastic snow replaced the real stuff ? Is this a flurry of misinformation ? Are all these people just flakes ? <h> All available evidence suggest snow @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ I understand why the Memphis council members would be suspicious . These videos are convincing , and they 're not AI nor the result of people deliberately hoaxing with prop snow . They are documents of what happens when you hold a flame up to real , actual , fell-from-the-sky snow . You 'd expect that holding fire to a snowball would make it melt into water in your hand but it just does n't . No shade to people running their own experiments , but they 're missing that snow can be counterintuitive . <h> Why it seems like snow does n't melt from flames <p> Snow is 90 -- 95% air , so there 's a lot less water than people might expect no matter how it melts . But the main thing going on is sublimation -- a solid changing directly to a gas without first becoming liquid . When you hold a flame to snow , especially packed snow , much of it will become water vapor without becoming liquid water first . Sublimation is also why snow can seem to disappear without the temperature going @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the video below . <p> Snow is also porous . When a snowball melts , water is sucked to the center of the mass through capillary action , and it fills up the spaces that were once air . The video below shows unpacked snow on the ground being hit with a torch . Some of the snow is sublimating in response to the heat , while some of the surface snow is melting into water and being suckedinto the empty spaces in the snow below it . You can see how it goes from " powdery " snow to more wet snow by the end of the video . ( Also , these yahoos are going to burn down the trailer soon ) : <h> But what about the snow turning black ? <p> The scorch marks on the " burning snow " have an explanation as well : The flame from a match or a lighter is result of fuel burning -- butane from a lighter ; wood or paper from matches . As the fuel burns , it produces carbon soot , which reacts to the cold @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't scorch marks from the snow burning . It 's scorch marks from the butane or wood/paper burning . You can tell the snow itself is n't burning , because it never catches fire . <p> That leaves only the burning plastic smell that some report . That 's actually the smell of the butane from the lighter not fully burning and/or the smell of the mercaptans sometimes added to butane so we can smell it . The result is a chemical odor that is easy to mistake for burning plastic , especially when you hold a flame up to soot you 've already deposited on a cold surface . In this video , the conspiracy theorist used a candle instead of a lighter , and notes that it does n't smell like burning plastic . That 's because butane was absent . <h> How to do the " burning snow " illusion yourself <p> You can try all this yourself to amaze your friends with the wonders of sublimation and/or trick a bunch of people on social media . It 's easy : <p> Grab some snow and pack @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will help soot stick to it . <p> Apply flame from a standard butane lighter for a few seconds . If you use matches , you wo n't get the same burning plastic smell . <p> Cool scorch mark , right ? Note how little water is dripping and how the snow is " disappearing . " <p> Note the edges of the scorch mark . Here 's where water that did melt was pulled toward the center of the snowball . <p> If you want to debunk the snow-burn conspiracy , simply hold the snow in your hand instead , and you will find that it melts into water . <h> Is it possible to make fake snow ? <p> What if the government wanted to create a fake snow storm for some reason ? It 's possible -- you can see fake snow at ski resorts during bad winters ; you can buy your own snow-maker on Amazon for less than $100 . The problem would be the scale . All " they control the weather " conspiracies fall apart when you consider the scale . <p> Artificial @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into air that 's below freezing . You could cover some trails at a ski resort without a problem , but a whole city or state would require a lot of snow . Industrial snow-making-machines use about 160,000 gallons of water to create one-acre-foot of snow . To cover a town that 's 25 square miles with six inches of snow , you 'd need about 1.28 billion gallons of water pumping through thousands of snow-guns . It would cost a lot , use a ton a fuel , and it would n't fool anyone anyway -- those machines are loud as hell , and the snow would n't fall from the sky ; it would shoot out of snow guns . You 'd end up like , " What am I even doing with my life ? " <h> Bottom line : We ca n't control the weather <p> Humankind can collectively alter weather patterns -- global climate change and all that -- but we ca n't control weather . We ca n't make it snow on command in Memphis without anyone noticing thousands of roaring machines shooting artificial @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hurricanes . @@134301106 <p> Washington appears to be a constant battlefield between the Trump administration and Democrats over every single issue . But below the surface , US politicians often take bipartisan approaches to important issues -- a fact that gets lost in the media 's need to portray everything as an existential struggle . <p> A surprising example has just come into the open . Last week , President Donald Trump signed an overwhelmingly bipartisan spending bill that restructures US diplomacy and development programs in significant ways . <p> This was unimaginable a year ago , when one of the biggest stories in Washington was the apparent end of the US foreign assistance program . The Trump administration abruptly closed the venerable US Agency for International Development , once the world leader in effective aid programs . In a chaotic house-cleaning , thousands of USAID employees were laid off , and many programs were terminated . What was left was merged into the State Department . <p> Trump 's task was made politically easier by the nature of some of the aid projects . Many Americans were surprised to learn that their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ musical in Ireland and a transgender comic book in Peru . <p> Elon Musk , as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency , seemed particularly intent on eliminating foreign assistance . He posted on his social media platform that ' USAID is a criminal organization . Time for it to die . ' <p> This kind of over-the-top rhetoric and the actual end of USAID produced justified outrage and a bleak outlook for the United States ' foreign aid leadership . British international charity Oxfam predicted that the loss of health and humanitarian programs caused by Trump 's aid cuts would mean three million unnecessary deaths each year . <p> Dire forecasts such as Oxfam 's were overstatements , but there has been genuine concern across the political spectrum that the US was losing an important foreign policy tool . Mitch McConnell , once the leader of Senate Republicans and a stalwart conservative , worried that aid cuts might give China an opportunity to win friends in the developing world as the US withdrew . <p> Trump 's aid-cutting efforts , particularly the shuttering of USAID , were @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ programs had become a partisan battleground years earlier . Policy battles over abortion , family planning , climate change and other programs linked to controversial political issues sucked up much of the attention and sapped the overall effort of its bipartisan support . <p> In 2024 , Trump campaigned on an inward-looking , build-up-America platform . Foreign assistance programs are tough to sell to US voters in the best of times , but almost impossible when domestic needs are seen as acute . After taking office last year , Trump followed through and revamped aid unilaterally -- without specific approval from Congress . Many called on Congress to oppose Trump 's actions . <p> Of course , the US Congress today is aligned with Trump . The vast majority of Republicans in Congress support Trump 's agenda and , when they do disagree on an issue , will raise objections behind closed doors so as not to give any succour to adversarial Democrats . Thus , calls for a Republican-majority Congress to actively oppose the president 's cuts to aid programs were never going to work . <p> One year @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Through its regular budgeting process , both Republicans and Democrats in Congress have given life to a slightly smaller and transformed US foreign assistance program . Last week , as part of a larger spending package , Trump signed into law a foreign assistance spending bill . This is a remarkable achievement in the current political environment . <p> Led by Mario Diaz-Balart , a strong Trump ally from South Florida , the new spending law provides for a foreign assistance program run out of the State Department at 86 percent of the Biden administration 's last budget . Diaz-Balart 's bill won votes from Freedom Caucus Republicans and progressive Democrats . <p> There will be some changes to US foreign aid programs , of course . Spending is modestly reduced across the board . Trump has more flexibility to use funds for non-traditional development programs , allowing him to offer transactional deals to developing countries in a manner that fits his style of diplomacy . This instrumentalisation of aid -- linking it directly to US national security -- will earn plenty of criticism from aid professionals , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ assistance programs . <p> Without USAID and with many aid professionals now gone from government service , the State Department will have to program billions of dollars with reduced accountability and monitoring tools . There are simply not enough people to effectively manage the programs . These challenges will have to be managed deftly . Assistance partnerships with allies such as Australia are now more important than ever . <p> The harsh rhetoric between Trump and Democrats will likely continue , but the critical story is where the two parties agree on new ways forward for US foreign policy . <p> Author <p> Lester Munson is a non-resident fellow with the United States Studies Centre .

By Andy Hazel . <h> Alexander Skarsg ? rd on love , sex and Pillion <p> Over the past two decades , Alexander Skarsg ? rd has embodied men who dominate rooms simply by standing in them . In roles such as the swaggering vampire Eric Northman in True Blood , the corporate brute Lukas Matsson in Succession or Amleth , the Viking warrior prince of The Northman , Skarsg ? rd 's steely gaze and luminous self-confidence has been a consistent screen presence . Even when those figures fracture , their power rarely does . <p> Pillion , his most unusual film to date , asks something else of him entirely . " When I heard ' BDSM relationship ' and ' biker culture ' , I expected something very different , " he says . " I did n't expect it to have so much sweetness and tenderness and awkwardness . " <p> In Pillion , Skarsg ? rd is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ whose presence is felt less through dialogue than through posture , restraint and a meticulously rationed smile . Opposite is Harry Melling , still recognisable from playing Dudley Dursley in the Harry Potter film series , who plays Colin , a polite , socially awkward traffic warden . The film contains scenes of explicit sex and kink , but the film is in essence a surprisingly gentle romantic comedy . <p> When Skarsg ? rd first read the script , Pillion was an unfinanced first feature from a virtually unknown director , Harry Lighton . " I ca n't take credit for the development process , " the 49-year-old actor says , " but Pillion felt tonally unlike anything I 'd ever read . It was so exciting and surprising to me . It was n't that I came in to finance it , I just said , ' Let 's see if there 's anything I can do to help that happen . ' ? " <p> Skarsg ? rd is drawn to stories that surprise him , which he says often come from the next generation of filmmakers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sake , he says , but in the space these films create for risk . I do n't want it to sound like an act of altruism that I attach my name to new filmmakers . Like with Pillion , I was n't like , ' Harry , let me help you on your career . " I often find sex scenes quite boring in movies because a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to two people hooking up -- or several people hooking up , as happens in our movie . Anger 's meld of motorbikes , silent , leather-clad men , pop music and Christian and Nazi imagery focused on surfaces and iconography , lavishing attention on its subjects in a way that still feels transgressive . <p> The 28-minute film proved so potent it became the subject of obscenity charges and lawsuits from both the Lutheran Church and the American Nazi Party , all of which failed . Similarly , in Pillion , Skarsg ? rd is a muscular man in tight leather who gives almost nothing away and whose very presence feels transgressive . <p> For all its leather , restraint and ritual , Pillion ultimately rests on what Ray is unable to conceal about himself , something Skarsg ? rd admits was part of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ he says . " So it 's all stipulated and clear at the beginning what the rules are . We wanted to avoid that because a lot of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trying to figure out his first venture into this type of relationship and what Ray expects of him . @@134334603 <h> Melania is an undeniable crock , the work of a hireling director so timid and apathetic he ca n't even capitalise on the political bifurcation in front of him . By Christos Tsiolkas . <h> Melania : all dressed up but going nowhere <p> The most obvious -- and the least interesting -- thing to say about the documentary Melania is that it is propaganda . Much more fascinating is the film 's critical reception since its release two weeks ago . The vitriol that has greeted the documentary in the press and online has been near uniform . <p> As the response has been so hostile , I should admit to a contrarian impulse before seeing it -- a hope that I would find the film entertaining as camp or at the very least informative about the current First Lady of the United States . I went in knowing nothing about Melania Trump 's background or even her origin story . I emerged after the screening knowing a few facts but having gleaned nothing enlightening about her . <p> She 's a figure who lives in the shadows @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- the vehement loathing and equally intense adoration -- that clings to her husband , Donald Trump . Melania keeps the First Lady front and centre of nearly every frame , but she never emerges from the gloom of contemporary American culture . <p> Does it matter what any critic says of this film ? I watched the movie in a suburban cinema during the first week of its release . There were seven other viewers , in itself not unusual for an early afternoon weekday screening . No cinema in Melbourne 's CBD or inner city was showing it . The bifurcation of popular culture is now endemic -- this is n't a film made for me or for anyone reading this newspaper . If there is any animus , any passion guiding the making of Melania , it is contempt for liberal audiences . A smarter , more dangerous right-wing filmmaker would have brought that detestation to the fore in their documentary . Director Brett Ratner is such an apathetic and timid hack that he shirks even that possibility . <p> The film is structured around the 20 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as president . The best part is the first 10 minutes , where we see Melania in discussion with designers and couturiers , assessing the outfits and accessories she will be wearing for Inauguration Day . <p> A former model and child of a Slovenian textile designer , Amalija Knavs , who worked in a state-owned clothing factory in the former Yugoslavia , Melania Trump is clearly knowledgeable about fashion . With her fingers gently tracing fabrics , as she expertly discusses the shape and fit of a dress or a skirt with a designer , her poise is undeniable . I wondered if the doco was going to sequester all current affairs from its purview and concentrate only on the sartorial and technical details of the preparations . That would have been an arguably radical choice . I doubt it would have satisfied those primed to hate Melania , but it might have made for a more provocative film . <p> The state of American documentary-making is wretched at a time when we are seeing the emergence of documentarians of real insight and provocation in the rest of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Ratner , a hireling director whose career was curtailed by #MeToo accusations , and also that it was financed by Amazon , there was little chance the documentary was ever going to be daring . Ratner has shown no sign of imagination or intellectual curiosity in any of his previous films , and the most generous thing one can say about Melania is that formally the cinematography has the crisp , saturated colour of advertisements for luxury products . In one sense , that is exactly what Melania is : an expensive advertisement to humanise the First Lady . <p> The film imitates the style of v ? rit ? documentary -- the pretence that the camera is observing its subject and her world , that we are privy to moments of intimacy and retreat . That 's certainly why those first 10 minutes are successful . As soon as Melania 's narration begins , the off-screen , stage-managed scripts that are controlling the production become obvious . <p> It 's a weakness that her voice is reedy and uninspiring . More unfortunately , Melania 's words are banal , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ when she is talking about her family -- the grief she has suffered with the recent death of her mother , or her affection for her son , Barron -- she sounds detached and unemotional . <p> This emotional emptiness is compounded by Ratner 's astonishing incuriosity . The upheavals of the former Yugoslavia , the trajectory that led Melania from a jobbing gig as a model to meeting Donald Trump , do n't seem to interest the director at all . There are no questions asked about her past . We glimpse a moment of intimacy between Melania and Tham Kannalikham , an interior designer originally from Laos who has worked on renovating the private quarters of the White House in both the Trump administrations . Both women offer the tritest of aspirational immigrant stories to the camera , but I wanted to know how their experiences of growing up in communist societies might have affected their conservative politics . <p> There 's only one scene in the movie that made me sit up : a video conversation between Melania and France 's First Lady , Brigitte Macron . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ common experiences of media hounding and disapprobation that perhaps led to the camaraderie that is obvious in their interaction . Ratner decides to skim over this sequence , not allowing the camera to sit with them and risk that some real emotion or truth might emerge from their discussion . <p> The sexism is dumbfounding . Here are two of the most powerful women in the world and Ratner is n't remotely interested in who they are and what they have to say . Even though he is only an extra in the film , Donald Trump is the true subject being canonised in this documentary . <p> If nothing is revealed beyond the mask of the First Lady 's face , the blame ca n't solely be laid at her feet , nor at the behind-the-scenes manipulations overseeing the production . Melania is a failure as a documentary and the responsibility for that lies with the filmmakers . <p> The state of American documentary-making is wretched at a time when we are seeing the emergence of documentarians of real insight and provocation in the rest of the world . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Kleber Mendon ? a Filho and Agnes Varda 's Faces Places ( 2017 ) are some of my most cherished films of the past decade . The trace of propaganda has always been a vexed yet integral part of documentary film , inevitable in a form that is so often energised by political engagement . Yet in the best documentaries -- and I certainly would include Mendon ? a Filho 's and Agnes Varda 's films in this category -- both the formal and intellectual explorations are rarely predetermined : we trust that we are discovering the subject alongside the filmmakers . <p> The best documentarians ask questions , including questions of themselves as filmmakers and observers . Ratner is n't interested in any of that . Neither , for that matter , are the lauded American documentarians Kirby Dick and Alex Gibney . Melania is a crock , but the gnashing scorn poured on it by critics is disingenuous . The emperor has n't been wearing any clothes for some time now . <p> Melania is screening in cinemas nationally . <p> This article was first published in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2026 as " Empty vessel " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@134337744 <p> In Patagonia 's dense forests , some trees tower above the rest . The largest have grown as tall as a 20-story building and are nearly as thick as a small school bus is long , surviving everything nature has thrown at them for thousands of years . But now , the world may have to watch them burn . <p> In early January , severe wildfires erupted in Argentina 's Patagonia region , tearing through scrubland and forest in Chubut Province . By mid-month , new fires had ignited in southern Chile . As crews struggled to contain the blazes , they spread across northern Patagonia and the Andean foothills of central-southern Chile -- killing 23 people , forcing tens of thousands to evacuate , and scorching dense native forests and national parks . <p> While the situation has somewhat improved , wildfires are still activelyburning in both countries . A report published today by World Weather Attribution -- a non-profit that quantifies how climate change influences the intensity and likelihood of a given natural disaster -- found that excessive heat , months of drought , and fierce @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> At the same time , these fires are destroying our best lines of defense against climate change : ancient forests . In Argentine Patagonia , the blazes are decimating large swaths of Los Alerces National Park , a UNESCO World Heritage Site famous for its ancient Alerce trees -- some of the oldest living trees on Earth . <h> A climate feedback loop <p> The park is home to the longest-living population of Alerce trees in the world , according to the UNESCO World Heritage Center . The oldest , largest specimen stands nearly 200 feet ( 60 meters ) tall and is estimated to be 2,600 years old . It could live another thousand years if it survives these fires -- the Alerce is the second-longest-living tree species in the world . <p> Over the course of their very long lives , these trees draw massive amounts of carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and store it in their biomass -- their trunk , branches , roots , and leaves . Research has shown that the largest 1% of trees store roughly half of the above-ground biomass @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ atmosphere directly mitigates the greenhouse effect , tempering the rise of global temperatures . <p> But when these giant trees burn , it 's basically like setting off a carbon bomb . Their stored carbon is released back into the atmosphere , fueling global warming and creating hotter , drier conditions that make wildfires more likely and severe -- as seen in the current crisis in Chile and Argentina . More forests burn , and the cycle starts over again . <p> All forest fires emit carbon dioxide , but the burning of ancient , massive trees releases far more than the burning of younger forests . At the same time , the destruction of expansive old-growth forests -- like those in Los Alerces National Park -- reduces terrestrial carbon storage capacity . <h> A devastating blow to conservation efforts <p> As Los Alerces burns , carbon emissions are n't the only cause for concern . The World Weather Attribution report states that the destruction of critical habitat is putting vulnerable species at risk , including the South Andean deer , the pud ? ( the world 's smallest deer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ protection of this forest is also vital for the conservation of the Alerce tree , which is itself a threatened species . <p> The report concludes that wildfire poses a growing threat to this world heritage site and the flora and fauna it protects . Across both the Chilean and Argentine regions affected by the current wildfire crisis , all climate models project a continued shift toward more severe fire weather conditions alongside declining seasonal rainfall . <p> " This strong agreement among models gives us high confidence that the changes already observed are driven by climate change , " the report states . <p> It 's too soon to say how much damage the forests of Los Alerces will sustain from these fires , but if the global temperature continues to rise unabated , humanity may be the force that finally kills the park 's millennia-old giants .
