@@134338363 <p> China is currently on track to completely retrofit its coal power fleet from baseload generation to flexibility support by 2027 , paving the way for its eventual exit from the country 's power system entirely . <p> This is the stunning conclusion reached by global energy think tank Ember , which reveals in a new report that China is on track to meet its national target of retrofitting almost its entire existing coal power fleet for flexible operation by 2027 . <p> As China enters the 15th FYP , Ember has found that steady progress over the past five years retrofitting its coal fleet has exceeded the original 2025 target , with 360 gigawatts ( GW ) of existing coal power capacity retrofitted for flexibility . <p> Along with new coal units that have been designed with greater operational range , China 's total flexible coal capacity exceeded 600 GW by the end of 2024 , and current policy signals indicate that retrofit potential across the existing fleet is on track to be largely realised within the next two years . <p> A similar transition is happening in Australia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- where possible -- to flex up to 80 per cent of their rated capacity . Or , in some cases , to be switched off altogether for periods in a strategy known as " two-shifting . " <p> " Shifting coal towards a flexibility role can fill in the gap in system support needed as renewables expand , while gradually reducing its strategic importance in the bigger picture , " said Biqing Yang , an energy analyst for Ember . <p> With a population of 1.4 billion in 2025 , China 's energy demands are huge , but even so , coal power generation still fell in China in 2025 , down 1.6 per cent to 46 terawatt-hours ( TWh ) , according to Carbon Brief . <p> Coal utilisation has also declined by more than 20 per cent over the past two decades , according to Ember , and , after a brief post-pandemic increase , continues to decline . <p> Driven by numerous policy mechanisms at the federal and state levels , China 's coal fleet is increasingly shifting to provide system flexibility and security , rather @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ share of the market . <p> Ember also reportes that by the end of 2025 China had installed 144.7 GW of battery storage , an 85 per cent year-on-year increase . <p> China 's efforts to deploy battery storage must keep pace with its levels of renewable energy generation , or risk relying too much on coal capacity to fill in the flexibility gap . <p> Battery @@134374436 <h> Sabrina Hahn : New CSIRO research sheds light on remarkable relationship between boronias and South West moth <p> Many West Australians will remember the fragrant bunches of brown boronia being sold as a cut flower in the city . Boronia megastigma has to have one of the most intoxicating perfumes in the plant kingdom . <p> Boronias have puzzled botanists for many years regarding their pollination process . The flowers are closed , making it extremely difficult for insects to effectively pollinate them . Making it even more of a challenge for pollinators , some of the anthers ( the male part ) are sterile , and the stigma ( the female part ) can be too large for certain insects to handle . <p> A team of researchers from CSIRO , led by Douglas Hilton , thought a small moth might be the mysterious pollinator of boronia flowers and began their research into the tiny Heliozelidae group of moths . They discovered there were thousands of Heliozelidae species in Australia , most of them unnamed . <p> A group of 15 Heliozelidae moth species in the South West @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with a particular species of boronia . One of these moth species was found exclusively on this specific boronia species . These moths have an intricate structure at the dorsal tip of their abdomen that collects pollen as the moth moves around the flower . <p> During spring , the female moth lays eggs inside the boronia flower . As she moves around the flower , the pollen collects in her abdomen . She will visit many flowers and spread the pollen as she goes . <p> The eggs hatch into caterpillars which eat the flowers and some of the seeds ; the caterpillar grows and pupates in the soil , making a cocoon , and emerging as a moth who visits the flowers -- and so the life cycle goes on . <p> For certain species , such as the brown boronia , moths may be the only visitors to their flowers . This indicates a reciprocal relationship where both the moth and the plant rely on each other for reproduction and , ultimately , for survival . This type of symbiotic relationship is reminiscent of the connection between @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ important for gardeners ? Many of us aim to eliminate caterpillars from our gardens , but studies on plant-insect relationships are still in their early stages . This scientific discovery highlights the vast amount we do n't yet understand . What we do know is that many of our native plants have intricate relationships that have evolved over hundreds of thousands of years . In some cases , a plant 's survival may depend entirely on a single species of insect , and vice versa . <p> With rapid deforestation due to mining and land clearing , along with climate change and inadequate environmental protection laws , biodiversity is declining at an alarming rate . We can never replace what has already been lost . <h> Tip of the week <p> When caterpillars are eating your plants , find out what they become , and let some develop into adulthood . They may be an important part of biodiversity survival in your garden . <p> Camera IconMulch can help plants during heatwaves . @@134408104 <h> Jo Tarnawsky The true cost of the AUKUS agreement <p> For several years now , the public debate around AUKUS has gone in familiar circles . How much will it cost ? Do the United States or the United Kingdom have the industrial capacity to meet their side of the arrangement ? Will the submarines arrive on time or at all ? <p> These are valid questions , but they are not the only ones we should be asking . The full cost of AUKUS ca n't be measured in budgets , delivery schedules or shipyard capacity alone . It must reckon with something less tangible but more consequential : Australia 's silence . <p> Within the Australian government , the US sits at the centre of defence and security thinking . It is embedded into the system 's DNA . Contemplating a world in which the alliance is weakened , conditional or unreliable is often dismissed as fantasy before it is genuinely examined . <p> Yet every day , the Trump administration is testing and , in some cases , tearing apart the rules-based international order . Power @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are ignored and multilateral guardrails are being treated as expendable . <p> Australia 's response is not simply one of diplomatic reserve . Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is pursuing a policy of deliberate restraint : avoiding unnecessary provocation , staying out of the spotlight and limiting commentary on America 's actions . Australia 's silence is its strategy . <p> The instinct is understandable . In the short term , it may even feel prudent and arguably in Australia 's immediate interest , but caution can easily be interpreted as indulgence and , over time , can harden into habit . <p> Australia 's centring of the US is visible not only in policy settings but in the physical spaces where power is exercised . The walls of the defence minister 's parliamentary office are lined with his enlarged photographs of American landmarks . Shelves are devoted to US history and politics , topped with White House memorabilia and gift-boxed flags from the Pentagon . Richard Marles 's ministerial office in Geelong displays a framed certificate signed by the then Kentucky governor when Marles was commissioned a Kentucky colonel . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and military figures travel with Marles on his flights . <p> These details are not incidental . They reflect how thoroughly the alliance is woven into Australia 's strategic identity and the psyche of those stewarding it . They provide a window into how unquestioned assumptions become default settings . <p> When an alliance becomes this embedded , it becomes difficult to question . Alternatives no longer feel conceivable , certain risks stop being interrogated and silence becomes the path of least resistance . <p> Within the Australian government , the US sits at the centre of defence and security thinking . It is embedded into the system 's DNA . Contemplating a world in which the alliance is weakened , conditional or unreliable is often dismissed as fantasy before it is genuinely examined . <p> The question is no longer whether American power and behaviour is changing but how long Australia can afford to behave as though it is n't . We are just weeks into the new year and US President Donald Trump has already made openly coercive threats against Greenland , deployed even harsher tariffs as weapons @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for international law . Australia 's public response has been cautious . Albanese routinely defaults to the position that he will not engage in a running commentary on US actions . Ministers rely on this to justify their silence , merely noting the government is " monitoring " developments . <p> Monitoring is not a strategy . Silence is not neutral . <p> It is against this backdrop that AUKUS takes on a far more urgent significance . <p> AUKUS is widely understood to be among the most consequential defence commitments Australia has undertaken , not simply because of its scale but because it binds future governments , budgets and strategic choices to assumptions formed in a world that is already fading . <p> The original controversy surrounding AUKUS was not technical , but political . The Morrison government 's abrupt abandonment of Australia 's submarine agreement with France ruptured trust and shocked many . By the time Labor came to office in May 2022 , the decision to proceed had already been accepted . The question became not whether to pursue AUKUS but how . <p> That work took @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ still-recognisable framework of alliance management , institutional process and strategic restraint . Decisions were made on the assumption that long-term commitments , once agreed , would be honoured through continuity rather than leverage . <p> That world no longer exists . <p> In a geopolitical environment characterised by transaction and volatility , long-term arrangements that depend on discretion and goodwill are inherently vulnerable . Silence does not stabilise such arrangements ; it leaves them exposed . Vague assurances to " trust us " are no longer sufficient for the billions of Australian taxpayer dollars being committed , nor for the widening capability gap now emerging , nor for the accumulating cost of silence that accompanies it . <p> Governments will routinely say of their defence settings that they are acting in the national interest . The question is how that interest is defined and over what time horizon . In moments of pressure , national interest is often narrowed to the avoidance of immediate risk . In a world where power is increasingly exercised through transaction and spectacle , however , silence may preserve surface stability only temporarily , while @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ security depends . <p> The consequences of this are obvious in ordinary life . Anyone who has encountered a playground bully understands the dynamic . One child is singled out , then another . Others sit under the tree nearby , eyes down , scuffing at the dirt , not because they approve of what is happening but because they hope not to be next . Silence , in that moment , creates the conditions in which the behaviour can continue . In fact , the bully relies on it . Each unchallenged incident makes the next one easier , more normal and less surprising . <p> In geopolitics , the stakes are higher but the logic is the same . Silence is not always read as restraint . More often , it is interpreted as tolerance . <p> Australia has shown that it can speak with clarity when it chooses to . The response to Russia 's invasion of Ukraine has been clear and sustained : naming aggression , imposing sanctions and framing the conflict explicitly as a breach of international law and sovereignty . The government has not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , where it believes principles and interests align . By contrast , when comparable questions have arisen about the conduct of the US -- including in Venezuela -- Australia 's public language has been muted . <p> This contrast matters . <p> It demonstrates that Australia does not lack the capacity for moral clarity nor for diplomatic firmness . What it lacks is the willingness to apply that same clarity when the uncomfortable behaviour is that of its most important ally . <p> This reluctance is nothing new . Australia has historically been cautious about publicly challenging the US , even when American actions have strained international law or divided global opinion . Former prime minister Malcolm Fraser warned of this dynamic more than a decade ago in Dangerous Allies , the book he wrote with Cain Roberts , arguing that Australia 's habit of outsourcing strategic judgement to " great and powerful friends " carried growing risks as global power shifted . <p> As a middle power , Australia is not without options . Among a number of world leaders reassessing old assumptions last month at the World Economic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the shift confronting middle powers with courage and clarity . The world order , he said , is not in transition , but rupture . Shared norms and institutional constraint can no longer be assumed . Carney warned that middle powers now face a blunt reality : if they are not at the table with one another -- setting the terms and acting collectively -- they are on the menu . <p> Carney was not calling for confrontation . He was calling for honesty about power , interests and the dangers of quiet compliance . He also made clear that Canada was adjusting its policies to reflect those realities . <p> There has been no comparable public recalibration as yet in Australia . <p> Carney 's warning was not that alliances are obsolete but that strong partnerships depend on agency -- the capacity to speak , to shape outcomes and to act collectively when norms are under strain . Australia does not lack credibility , capability or standing . What is missing is the willingness to use these openly in a rapidly changing world and with regard to a great @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ alliance is meant to uphold . <p> Australia continues to meet the US schedule of downpayments for the promised submarines , already in multiple billions of dollars . The success or failure of AUKUS will eventually be measured in submarines delivered and capability realised for the money spent . Its deeper cost is already being incurred . <p> Silence may buy time . It may keep attention at bay for a while . But in an era where power is exercised openly and without apology , silence is not a shield . @@134408120 <h> Helen Haines Who 's paying for the Coalition melodrama <p> Since the last election , Australia has witnessed the biggest political on-again , off-again break-up of the 21st century . The one great exception to this unfortunate pattern is " national security " , which is always defined in terms of comparative military capabilities and always ruinously expensive . As the ill-starred AUKUS project reminds us , the exception does n't inspire confidence in the rule . <p> But what if we looked backwards for inspiration rather than forwards ? Getting a stronger sense of the context in which our collective destiny is unfolding might provide a useful reminder of the nature of nature and the very material challenges we face . <p> It 's not necessary to go back to the Big Bang nearly 14 billion years ago for this to be an interesting and illuminating exercise , but as unresolved @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 'm not expecting our Prime Minister to explain what caused the Big Bang or why we are part of a cosmos that is apparently still expanding at 73 kilometres per second . However , the important time frame for us is " only " 3-4 billion years ago when life began on Earth . Human ancestors started to appear around seven million years ago , but the development of agriculture and " civilisation " began incredibly recently : a mere 1,200 years ago . <p> Our development as the world 's dominant life form has only gathered pace ever since . Since we became conscious and able to think , there 's been no stopping us . Whether the equally rapid expansion of the human population should be judged as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ indicator of the limits of our ability to act collectively in an environmentally or even politically sustainable manner is another question , but not one that 's asked as often as we might hope or expect . <p> What we can say is that some of the most profound historical changes that have shaped contemporary reality have not been the carefully considered product of enlightened leadership . On the contrary , the rise of nation-states , the development of capitalism , and the industrial revolution have all been the product of experimentation and the evolution of patterns of social behaviour that favoured some outcomes over others . <p> The question that emerges from a sense of our remarkable , shared and collectively determined history is : are we any better placed to consciously shape a sustainable future for coming generations than we have been in the past ? <p> The evidence is not encouraging . " Exhibit A " is our collective inability to stop killing other people who look or act differently , have things we want , or have different beliefs about the origins of the universe and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> No doubt it was ever thus . And yet there have been relatively uninterrupted periods of relative peace and prosperity , especially in places like Australia . True , they may have been as much a product of luck as good judgement , but they do suggest that progress is possible and not just the material variety either . <p> There are still optimists who think that it 's still possible if , as Barack Obama famously suggested , we simply stop doing stupid shit . Perhaps I 'm hopelessly naive , but spending less on armaments and more on global climate change mitigation might be an obvious place to reconsider our priorities , all other things being equal . <p> Unfortunately , things are notoriously unequal . Not only is wealth increasingly concentrated , but so , too , is the capacity to make the choices that will define our collective future . Perhaps it will figure out how to " save the planet " , too . Who knows , perhaps AI 's the next step in a long-running evolutionary process . <p> Whatever the answer to such questions , history suggests that human beings are n't likely to come up with a carefully considered , future-oriented collective response to a rapidly changing world . The most consequential historical change in this regard is our unprecedented capacity to blow ourselves to pieces , by accident or intent . <p> Perhaps AI will sort that out , too . @@134497856 <p> For decades , antibiotics have been humanity 's frontline defense against bacterial infections , yet these essential medications have also led to the rise of drug-resistant " superbugs . " Now , researchers have discovered an ancient strain of bacteria that managed to develop this superpower thousands of years before humans ever invented antibiotics . <p> A study published Tuesday in the journal Frontiers in Microbiology describes Psychrobacter SC65A.3 , a bacterial strain discovered frozen inside 5,000-year-old layers of cave ice in Romania . Testing revealed that SC65A.3 is resistant to 10 modern antibiotics and carries more than 100 genes linked to resistance despite never being exposed to these drugs . <p> " Studying microbes such as Psychrobacter SC65A.3 retrieved from millennia-old cave ice deposits reveals how antibiotic resistance evolved naturally in the environment , long before modern antibiotics were ever used , " co-author Cristina Purcarea , a senior scientist at the Institute of Biology Bucharest of the Romanian Academy , said in a release . <h> Ancient superbug unearthed <p> Antibiotic resistance is an urgent threat to global public health . In the U.S. alone , more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more than 35,000 people die as a result , according to the CDC 's 2019 Antibiotic Resistance Threats Report . <p> This threat has grown in tandem with the rise of antibiotic use . Antibiotic resistance is a classic example of natural selection : when microbes are exposed to a drug , most die , but a few survive thanks to protective genetic traits . Those survivors then pass their resistance genes onto the next generation , which passes them on to the next , giving rise to superbugs . <p> While exposure to antibiotics amplifies the prevalence of resistance genes , it does not imbue microbes with these protective traits . Those arise naturally through random genetic mutations and the constant pressure to out-perform other microorganisms in the environment , many of which produce their own antimicrobial compounds . <p> The ancient Psychrobacter SC65A.3 strain is a perfect example of how these natural processes lead to antibiotic resistance . Purcarea and her colleagues found it inside an 82-foot ( 25-meter ) ice core they extracted from Scarisoara Ice Cave in northwestern Romania . The core represents 13,000 years of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ SC65A.3 . <p> In the lab , the researchers isolated various bacterial strains from the core and sequenced their genomes to determine which genes allowed the strain to survive such low temperatures and which promote antimicrobial resistance . When they tested SC65A.3 against 28 widely used antibiotics , they found it was resistant to more than a third of them . <p> " The 10 antibiotics we found resistance to are widely used in oral and injectable therapies used to treat a range of serious bacterial infections in clinical practice , " including tuberculosis , colitis , and urinary tract infections , Purcarea explained . <h> High risk , high reward <p> The findings underscore a frequently overlooked public health threat associated with climate change , according to the study 's authors . <p> " If melting ice releases these microbes , these genes could spread to modern bacteria , adding to the global challenge of antibiotic resistance , " Purcarea said . As the global temperature rises , the risk of releasing ancient superbugs into the environment grows . Studying these bacterial strains , however , can also lead @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inspire new drugs and other biotechnological innovations , Purcarea noted . <p> The SC65A.3 genome contains 11 genes that may be able to kill or stop the growth of other bacteria , fungi , and viruses , for example . It also contains nearly 600 genes with unknown functions , suggesting that many more novel biological mechanisms could be hiding in this superbug 's DNA . <p> " These ancient bacteria are essential for science and medicine , " Purcarea said , " but careful handling and safety measures in the lab are essential to mitigate the risk of uncontrolled spread . "

@@134533076 <p> Sharks prowl nearly every marine ecosystem on Earth -- except one . For decades , scientists assumed the waters around Antarctica were simply too cold to sustain these predators , but a surprise sighting is challenging that belief . <p> Scientists with the Minderoo-UWA Deep-Sea Research Centre , based in Western Australia , were operating an undersea camera off the South Shetland Islands near the Antarctic Peninsula when a southern sleeper shark glided into view . The specimen , filmed in January 2025 , was spotted more than 1,600 feet ( 490 meters ) beneath the sea surface . At that depth , the water temperature was just 35.6 degrees Fahrenheit ( 2 degrees Celsius ) , according to the Research Centre . <p> " That was certainly very unexpected , " Heather Stewart , a senior researcher and associate professor at the Deep-Sea Research Centre , said in a March 2025 video about the sighting . " In terms of geographic distribution , this species has not actually been seen within Antarctic waters . This is the most southerly that this seems to have been found , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ southern sleeper shark is a large , slow-moving species of deepwater shark typically found across the Southern Ocean from central Chile to the sub-Antarctic Islands . While it is well adapted to cold temperatures , it 's still rare to see this species venture into the frigid waters immediately surrounding Antarctica . <p> The Southern Ocean is heavily stratified , with vertical water layers that change in temperature and salinity according to their depth . The sleeper shark caught on camera maintained a depth of roughly 1,600 feet along a seabed that sloped into deeper water . This is a relatively warmer layer , providing a hospitable " corridor " that allowed this specimen to venture south of its geographic range , according to the Minderoo-UWA Deep-Sea Research Centre . <p> While this is the first photographic evidence of a shark in this region , this specimen likely is n't alone . Alan Lamieson , founding director of the Research Centre , told the Associated Press that other Antarctic sharks probably live at the same depth , taking advantage of the warm layer to feed on whales , giant squid @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ seafloor . <h> The potential role of climate change <p> Peter Kyne , a Charles Darwin University conservation biologist who was not part of the team that captured video of this shark , told the AP that warming oceans due to climate change may be driving sharks toward Antarctica . Studies have shown that the distributions of numerous marine species -- including sharks -- have shifted as a result of rising ocean temperatures , with some research suggesting climate change could make Antarctica hospitable to sharks . <p> But impacts vary widely by species , and Kyne noted that there is limited data on range changes near Antarctica because the region is so remote . As such , the role climate change plays in pushing sharks farther south remains unclear . <p> The historic documentation of a shark in Antarctic waters begs for more research to investigate their prevalence in this region . Future findings could offer valuable insight into how climate change -- or other environmental pressures -- is reshaping the Antarctic Ocean 's ecology . 
@@134533110 <p> For a long time , scientists knew of a " gravity hole " beneath Antarctica -- an area with particularly weak gravitational force . Considering the various threats currently faced by the region , scientists are hoping to understand this anomaly better . At last , they may have a new lead . <p> Perhaps unsurprisingly , any shifts in Antarctica 's gravity overlap with major shifts in the region 's climate and geology . A historical analysis of Antarctica 's gravity hole , detailed in a recent Scientific Reports paper , explains that the hole started off weaker but grew stronger between 50 and 30 million years ago , when widespread glaciation took over Antarctica . <p> However , the team has yet to ascertain whether and how the gravity hole could impact Antarctica , especially as the effects of climate change worsen each year . <h> Not all spots are equal <p> The geoid is the bumpy , irregular ocean surface shaped by Earth 's gravitational influence . For instance , water tends to flow toward areas of stronger gravity , so sea levels in regions with relatively lower gravity , like Antarctica , are typically lower than expected . <p> The " low " here refers to a " broad depression in Earth 's gravity field caused by a deficit of mass at depth , " explained the researchers in a release from the Paris Institute of Earth Physics . <h> Tracking gravity 's path <p> For the study , the team reconstructed the 3D structure inside Earth using global earthquake recordings and " seismic , geodynamic , and mineral-physics data , " according to the paper . The team 's model accounted for elements such as mantle dynamics , gravity field data , and changes to Earth 's rotational behavior . <p> " Imagine doing a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't have X-rays like we do in a medical office . We have earthquakes , " Alessandro Forte , the study 's senior author and a geophysicist at the University of Florida , said in a university statement . " Earthquake waves provide the ' light ' that illuminates the interior of the planet . " <p> The researchers then used a similar technique to " rewind the flow of rocks in the interior and track changes back 70 million years , " according to the statement . The simulations revealed that initially , a cold , dense material sinking into the deep mantle drove the gravity low near Antarctica . <p> Then , between roughly 50 and 30 million years ago , hotter , lighter mantle began rising from deep inside , redistributing mass across the continent . The combination of the cold , sinking mantle and the hot , rising mantle amplified the overall deficit of mass below Antarctica , the study explained . <h> Things that sink <p> Since sea levels and tide dynamics subsequently influence climate patterns , researchers believe that better understanding the gravity hole @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- especially given the threats looming over the region today . <p> " If we can better understand how Earth 's interior shapes gravity and sea levels , we gain insight into factors that may matter for the growth and stability of large ice sheets , " Forte said .

@@134566047 <h> Is ' Wuthering Heights ' a new low for Hollywood ? <p> In our economy of diminishing returns , equality perhaps means that women are finally free to be just as good as men at making really , really bad art . This was my first thought after seeing Emerald Fennell 's " Wuthering Heights " . <p> Against the backdrop of the Yorkshire Moors , Catherine Earnshaw ( Margot Robbie ) -- precocious , truculent and ambitious -- grows up in a state of heightened sexual yearning alongside the brooding and earnest adopted Heathcliff ( Jacob Elordi ) . " Wuthering Heights " continues in the same course as Promising Young Woman and Saltburn , marketing itself as radically bold , sexually charged and visually impressive . ' s novel as a 14-year-old . It is a novel that has little to do with corset-ripping , lightweight BDSM or love , because Wuthering Heights is , among other things , about something far darker : the impossibility of love itself . <p> Beyond its complex social critique , it is also a novel that operates on the level of dream -- where reality is observed at oblique angles and defamiliarised to the point of grotesquerie in order to capture something about its essential , everyday strangeness . While most adaptations recast the novel @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Abismos de pasi ? n and Yoshishige Yoshida 's Arashi ga oka do a commendable job in interpreting the senseless cruelty of Bront ? ' s vision . @@134569056 <p> For years , the Faraglioni di Sant'Andrea -- an assemblage of limestone off the Adriatic near Italy -- has witnessed countless kisses , proposals , and other declarations of love . The continued stress on the rock formations likely led to the collapse , authorities said . <p> " It is a devastating blow to the heart , " Melendugno mayor Maurizio Cisternino told local reporters at Corrier Salentino ( translated from Italian ) . " <h> Mourning a historical landmark <p> The Faraglioni di Sant'Andrea was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ among couple visitors . @@134601904 <p> In Europe , avalanches have already killed more than 90 people since October in one of the deadliest seasons in years , European Avalanche Warning Services figures show , compared with only 36 people in the same time period last year . France and Italy have borne the brunt , with dozens of avalanche-related deaths since the start of this year . <p> Avalanches have also featured among Japan 's severe run of snow country deaths this year , alongside blizzards and chairlift accidents . <p> Advertisement <p> But what causes avalanches , and is climate change making it worse ? <h> Two types of avalanches <p> There are two types of avalanches . The first is a " loose snow avalanche " , when surface-level snow moves downhill from a single point . The second is a " slab avalanche " , which are much less predictable and more dangerous . <p> Members of a rescue team in Soda Springs , California.AP <p> Craig Sheppard , program manager for the Mountain Safety Collective , says this is caused by the interaction of the different layers in a snowpack @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in weather , it allows the crystals to change , and depending on what the weather is , they 'll change in different ways -- some weather will make the snow grains stronger , some weather will make the snow grains weaker , " Sheppard says . " If you get a weak layer underneath a strong layer , then that is a recipe for avalanches . " <p> When it does not snow for some time , the surface snow is exposed to warming during the day and colder temperatures at night , and it can form " facets " or weak crystals . When there is a fresh snow dump , it remains as an unstable layer below the surface . <p> The avalanche that killed two men in the Couloir Vesses , a well-known freeride route in Courmayeur , in the upper Val Veny , northern Italy.Italian Alpine Rescue via AP <p> " It forms these really feathery crystals , and they 're very beautiful , very delicate , but they stand up tall and it 's like standing up a deck of cards on their end @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ says . " Then you 're putting the next snowfall on these feathery crystals , and you obviously have a recipe for avalanches because you have snow sitting on a really weak grain . " <p> Or as Tyson Millar , an accredited avalanche safety expert from Protect Our Winters , a group that campaigns on the effect of climate change on the snow season , describes it : " That faceted snow is almost akin to having ball bearings in the layers of snow . " <p> Advertisement <p> This is exactly what occurred in Europe and the West Coast of North America this season , Millar says , because there was barely any snow fall for most of January , followed by dumps in February . Japan , by contrast , has had heavy snowfall all season . <h> Terrain for avalanches <p> Avalanches are less common in Australia because it is " maritime snowpack " , meaning the climate is affected by the proximity of the ocean . This is in contrast with the intercontinental or continental snowpacks that occur further inland in places such as the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they do n't happen with the same frequency as the intercontinental or continental snowpack , " Sheppard says . <p> Advertisement <p> The dangers in Australia lean more towards whiteout conditions that can cause people to become disoriented , and surface crusts on steep , icy slopes that can lead to hazardous " slide for life conditions " , he says . <p> Millar says New Zealand and coastal North American resorts such as Whistler in Canada are also considered maritime snowpack . However , despite being an archipelago , Japan gets a lot of wind off Siberia rather than warm , moist ocean air . <p> Associate Professor Nathalie Vriend at the University of Colorado Boulder writes inThe Conversation that slopes between 25 and 40 degrees run the greatest risk of avalanches . <p> Rescue crews work work at the site of an avalanche site in the ski resort of Crans-Montana , Switzerland in 2019 . AP <p> " Those are also ideal for skiing , of course , " Vriend says . " If the slope is less than 25 degrees , there might be little slips , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it 's over 40 degrees , the snow typically can not accumulate , clearing away the avalanche risk . " <p> Advertisement <h> Changing climate <p> Global warming could make avalanches less common because there is less snow . However , there are other ways that climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of avalanches . <p> Professor Steven Sherwood at the University of NSW Climate Change Research Centre says ski seasons are getting shorter nearly everywhere in the world because of higher temperatures . <p> " The snow is becoming more variable , in the sense that they can still get really big dumps , but they 're probably coming less often , and the snow is n't lasting as long , and also because they 're getting a higher fraction of rain to snow , " Sherwood says . <p> Advertisement <p> The lower altitudes would get more rain -- including rain falling on snow -- and moving up the mountain , the snow could be softer , he says . <h> Related Article <p> Sheppard says variability of snow seasons with long periods of no snowfall @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are all factors that increase avalanche risk . <p> A 2018 paper in PNAS found an increase in avalanche activity in the Himalayas was linked to contemporaneous climate warming , contradicting " the intuitive assumption that warming results in less snow , and thus fewer snow avalanches in the region " . <p> A 2024 peer-reviewed article in Nature Reviews Earth &amp; Environment says climate change could influence the " number , magnitude , flow regime , release , flowing snow type and seasonality of avalanches , as well as the types of terrains prone to avalanches " . <p> Advertisement <p> The paper reported a projected increase in wet avalanches -- usually a result of thaw conditions where slushy snow slides over bonded snow -- in the French Alps , central Rocky Mountains and western Norway . More data was needed to fully understand the impact of climate change on avalanche risk , including indirect factors such as the rise of the treeline or the retreat of the glaciers , the researchers said .

@@134637770 <h> Australia 's human tissue acts are set for their first overhaul in 50 years , in a move that is hoped to remove hurdles to donation and medical and research innovation . By Kristina Kukolja . <h> The reform to boost organ donation <p> An overhaul of the rules governing the use of human tissue looks increasingly likely as the Australian Law Reform Commission embarks on reform that is hoped to boost historically low organ donation rates . <p> This is the first review since the ALRC 's 1977 report , which underpins the human tissue acts . Given how much has changed over the past half century in medicine , technology and community attitudes , the starting point now is to legally define human tissue and whether that should take into account substances such as human milk , foetal and faecal tissue and " newly engineered materials that include human cells or cell lines " , according to the discussion paper . <p> The " most difficult and sensitive " question , says the ALRC 's Dr Maeghan Toews , who is co-leading the inquiry , will be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . " The concept of death raises not only legal but ... spiritual and philosophical issues that people have different views on . " <p> For the medical and research communities -- and especially the organ and tissue donation and transplant sector , which is a major focus of the review -- the outcome has implications for ethical oversight , consent and the medical interventions that patients and donated organs and tissue can be subjected to . It 's hoped reforms will help lift donation rates -- only about a third of Australians were registered organ or tissue donors in 2024 , according to the latest available data , and the national consent rate was 53 per cent , well below pre-Covid levels . The slow recovery is attributed in part to uncertainty among families of the deceased about whether they would have consented to donation . <p> Specifically , changing the definition of death would remove legal barriers that currently prevent hospitals in Australia from using international technology -- known as normothermic regional perfusion ( NRP ) -- that preserves donated organs , particularly livers , in the body @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of available organs for transplant , says Angela Webster , who is a professor of epidemiology at the University of Sydney and a transplant physician at Westmead Hospital . <p> " Up to 20 per cent of the organs that we currently do n't use , but have considered for use , could be trialled " using NRP , says Webster . <p> As part of a wider focus on making organ and tissue transplant more equitable , Toews says , the review is also consulting on ways to address the " disparity in access to kidney transplants for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people " and recommendations to avoid " unintended negative consequences " for Indigenous people and research participants in light of the " long history of taking tissue from First Nations communities without consent for research and educational purposes " . <p> It 's also working to identify if there are " specific rules " that should be introduced " to help restore trust from First Nations communities in Australian medical research " . <p> Another benefit of reform to ensure the ethical and efficient use of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sovereign research capacity and reduce reliance on overseas jurisdictions , particularly at a time when public trust in science is under pressure in some countries " , says Louise Baur , president of the Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences . <p> " How do we make sure the changes recognise the ethical issues and the respect for donors , but do n't create such incredible hurdles that we 're doing ourselves out of innovation or imposing higher levels of regulation than what happens elsewhere . " <p> Australian health and medical researchers are still coming to grips with the impact of US government funding cuts to joint projects under the Trump administration , and the uncertainty that has caused . The directives to pull back on diversity , equity and inclusion efforts and cuts to scientific funding and personnel in key government health agencies have had international consequences . There are calls from within the sector for Australia to diversify research funding sources , ahead of this year 's expected release of an updated National Health and Medical Research Strategy , which aims to strengthen Australia 's domestic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the ALRC 's discussion paper , released late last year , are the creation of a national legislative framework and an overarching national regulator . This would " harmonise and modernise " the " complex , fragmented and nationally inconsistent framework of oversight , guidance and legislation " across Commonwealth , state and territory jurisdictions , according to the Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences submission paper . <p> " Some states and territories have different rules about what is and is n't allowed before and after death , or in that dying phase , and that could impact how well those organs work , " says Webster . <p> Webster says at Westmead Hospital three transplant patients from different states are receiving organs from interstate donors even as she speaks to The Saturday Paper . <p> " We ca n't ever even assume what we 're getting . We just do n't know . " <p> The proposed national regulator would operate either as a standalone body or integrate with existing groups such as the Organ and Tissue Authority , the National Blood Authority and the Therapeutic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of practice , standards and guidelines in clinical practice . <p> While she welcomes the prospect of streamlined regulation , Webster says there is concern the new legal framework may " seek to encroach or seep into clinical practice guidelines " . <p> In the health and medical research sector -- another review priority -- the " disparate " human tissue acts have created " layers of complexity " for researchers , says Dianne Nicol , distinguished professor of law and a fellow of the Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences . <p> Nicol , who is also on the ALRC advisory committee , says there 's heightened concern among researchers about the use of personal information , leading to " self-regulation " out of fear of breaching state or Commonwealth laws . <p> " Genetic technology has improved so much that any human tissue has a person 's DNA in it and it 's possible to sequence and identify the person , so it is much more likely that tissue can be identifiable back to an individual or to their family even if it was donated anonymously , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ addressed in the Privacy Act , and the issue is linked to questions of consent and ownership . <p> " There 's huge uncertainty whether human tissue is something that is capable of being owned , and , if so , whether it 's owned by the person that it comes from . There are exceptions , for example , if you preserve the tissue , it goes from something that ca n't be owned to something that can . " <p> That could have unaddressed legal and other implications , particularly for the operation of Australian biobanks -- from those administered by individual researchers to the new national Australian Health Biobank established by the CSIRO . <p> One solution the ALRC proposes is to create a " novel " legal consent right for tissue donors , says Commissioner Toews . " There has to be a right for participants to be able to access information about how their tissue is being used and to be able to withdraw consent for future research projects . " <p> Nicol says there is concern too about alignment between domestic and international regulatory @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ through human tissue laws but it 's less clear what the situation is when they 're importing human tissue . @@134637778 <h> Richard Denniss Why a teals party is a bad idea <p> As a former political staffer and an economist , there are two questions I hear a lot . One is , why do governments give so much of our gas away free ? The other is , should the " teals " form a political party ? The second is simple : no , it 's a terrible idea . The first answer takes a bit longer . The two questions are , however , inextricably linked . <p> To start with the idea of a new political party : this is the last thing Australia needs , whatever its branding or positioning . @@134637779 <h> Marcia Langton What should a writers ' festival be ? <p> There are cultural events that entertain , and there are rare ones that reorganise how a society encounters ideas . The Jaipur Literature Festival is the latter . Founded in 2006 by Namita Gokhale , William Dalrymple and Sanjoy Roy at Diggi Palace , the festival draws hundreds of thousands of people in person and tens of millions online . <p> Yet its magnetism lies not in scale alone . It rests on a curatorial philosophy that treats ideas as public life -- dynamic , contested , interdisciplinary and sensorial . Books are catalysts for encounters -- between novelists , political analysts , historians , scientists , politicians , economists and technologists . <p> The grace of the festival , as Gokhale puts it , is not softness but confidence in the public 's capacity for complexity . The authors , their books and their ideas are paramount . The festival does not succeed because it offers limitless free speech ; it succeeds because its founders and an enormous team of moderators , volunteers and cultural practitioners practice @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is constructed as a negotiated cultural common , where brilliance thrives because of orchestration . This is not an open mic of outrage nor a bureaucratically sanitised forum . It is a designed intellectual ecosystem where excellence , disagreement and complexity are actively cultivated . <p> This is the paradox contemporary culture often refuses to confront : scale produces influence ; influence attracts power ; and only strong curatorial leadership can keep ideas central rather than subordinated to chaos or institutional fear . William Dalrymple 's history factory , as I call it , was ever-present , and his presentations thrilling . <p> The contrast with Australia could not be clearer . The collapse of two writers ' festivals in Australia -- Adelaide Writers ' Week , the country 's oldest , and the Bendigo Writers Festival -- following mass boycotts by scheduled speakers after board and sponsor censorship , will drive cash-strapped festivals to ensure that speakers are safe and conversations are pre-approved . <p> In Australia , controversy is treated as an institutional failure rather than cultural vitality . The result is a narrowing of ambition , purpose @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ door is opened to mediocrity . In this climate , festivals will increasingly resemble risk-managed civic programming : cautious , polite , predictable . <p> Jaipur 's success rests precisely on refusing that timidity by engineering and curating a genuinely complex program . <p> One of the festival 's strengths is its capacity to elevate literary excellence while situating it within urgent social realities . Among the most compelling presences this year was Banu Mushtaq , whose collection Heart Lamp , translated by Deepa Bhasthi , won the International Booker Prize in 2025 . <p> Mushtaq 's stories explore patriarchy , caste and class with emotional precision . In the 1980s , a mother and her 16-year-old daughter live together above a hairdresser 's shop in an island town in Denmark . The daughter is starting high school and just starting to make new friends -- a group of adolescent misfits whom her circle will shortly widen to contain . At the centre of her quotidian , achingly detailed existence lies her mother . Their lives are in close orbit , enmeshed with one another and attuned to quiet daily rhythms and rituals . When the mother receives @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Rather the quality of their attention and the comfort they take in each other 's company intensifies , knowing the latter can not last . Browne is determined to break down patriarchal capitalism , so that women -- historically seen as financially incompetent -- feel empowered and educated enough to pursue financial independence . To this end , she incorporates her own story : penniless after divorce in her 30s , to multi-millionaire businesswoman , as well as the stories of other women . Part of this requires women to have faith in themselves , to be the " heroine " of their own stories . In entertaining writing , she goes into the nitty-gritty of making money ( not to be considered a dirty word ) . It reads like a coach revving up the team , but is also full of practical advice learnt over years .

@@134729056 <p> ? ? Often called the " lungs of Africa , " the Congo Basin is the world 's largest land-based carbon sink . For thousands of years , its swamps and peatlands have played a key role in regulating the global climate by soaking up vast amounts of carbon , but now , a troubling shift may be underway . <p> A study published Monday in the journal Nature Geoscience found that two lakes within the Basin -- Lac Mai Ndombe and its smaller neighbor , Lac Tumba -- are releasing carbon in the form of planet-warming carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) . While some of the CO2 comes from recently produced plant matter , up to 40% stems from the Basin 's ancient peat . <p> The swamps and peatlands of the Congo Basin only cover 0.3% of Earth 's land surface , but they hold 30 billion metric tons of carbon -- one-third of the amount stored across all tropical peatlands . Scientists have long assumed that this carbon would remain locked inside the peat for millennia , but these new findings suggest otherwise . <p> " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , that is the 30-billion-tonne question ! " lead author Travis Drake , a carbon biogeochemist at ETH Z ? rich , told Gizmodo in an email . " It is entirely possible that this is a natural , balanced cycle : The vast peatlands slowly release carbon from below while sequestering a comparable amount from above , resulting in no net loss , " Drake explained . " However , the more alarming possibility is that climate or land-use changes are actively destabilizing the system , causing it to lose its stored carbon . " <h> 150 gigatons of ancient carbon each year <p> The role that the Congo Basin 's peatlands play in regulating the global carbon cycle , and thus the climate , is poorly understood . That 's largely because the central part of the Basin is difficult for researchers to access due to a lack of road infrastructure . To overcome this , Drake and his colleagues used the natural waterways as their highway . <p> Traveling aboard a large ship that served as both their living quarters and a floating laboratory , they navigated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? -- to reach the southern point of Lake Mai Ndombe . <p> Both Mai Ndombe and Tumba are large , shallow blackwater lakes surrounded by swamp forests with thick peat deposits underneath . " Blackwater " is a colloquial term for a river or lake with a high concentration of dissolved organic matter , which gives the water a deep brown color resembling strong tea , Drake explained . The subsurface peat layer has accumulated over thousands of years as plant material has sunk to the wetland floor and partially decomposed . <p> The researchers collected and analyzed water samples from both lakes , finding that 39% of the carbon in Lake Mai Ndombe and 40% in Lake Tumba comes from peat . This suggests that the breakdown of long-stored peat is a significant source of CO2 emissions from these lakes . The researchers estimate that Lake Mai Ndombe alone may be releasing more than 150 gigatons of ancient carbon into the atmosphere each year . <h> A potential climate feedback loop <p> How this carbon is escaping from the peatlands remains unclear , but Drake 's team believes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ organic layer . <p> As microbes feed on the stored carbon , they convert it into methane through a process called methanogenesis . The researchers suspect that this subsurface methane then travels up through deep soil flowpaths into the lake , where it reacts with oxygen to produce CO2 . <p> " While we have found isotopic evidence in the lake supporting this , we still need to investigate the internal peat dynamics to confirm the full pathway , " Drake said . <p> It 's possible that climate change is also playing a role in mobilizing carbon from the peat . As rising global temperatures drive more frequent and prolonged droughts , this could cause the peatlands to partially dry out , exposing them to more oxygen and promoting rapid decomposition , Drake explained . <p> " There is actually paleoenvironmental evidence from regional peat cores showing that a similar climate-driven destabilization event has happened in the past , leading to massive losses of organic carbon , " he said . <p> If human-driven warming has led to a similar event today , a feedback loop may be taking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an event today would exacerbate climate change , though still to a lesser degree than the anthropogenic emissions currently driving the rapid buildup of CO2 in our atmosphere , " Drake explained . <p> He and his colleagues worry that rising temperatures and land use change could transform the Congo Basin 's blackwater lakes into sources of greenhouse gases , but how close they are to reaching this potential tipping point remains unclear . Their next project , which will investigate the mechanisms behind their findings and how these carbon emissions have evolved over the past 12,000 years , could offer some insight . <p> " Ultimately , our goal is to better constrain the carbon budget of these peatlands , establishing a baseline to assess future changes and determine their current stability , " Drake said .

@@134729752 <h> The environmental benefits and drawbacks of E10 fuel <p> E10 fuel has gained traction in some corners because of its environmental benefits . However , as with all sources of energy , it also has its challenges . <p> This article discusses the benefits and drawbacks of E10 fuel and how to balance them . <h> Benefits of E10 fuel <p> So , what is E10 fuel ? It is a new regular grade petrol that contains up to 10 per cent ethanol . Ethanol is a renewable energy source made from plant materials . It has a lower carbon footprint compared to regular gasoline . As the plants that will become biofuel grow , they repeatedly absorb more carbon dioxide than what will be emitted during fermentation and combustion , partially offsetting the greenhouse gas emissions from E10 fuel 's production and use . <p> Another benefit would be the reduction of harmful pollutants . Carbon monoxide and other toxic compounds are emitted at lower levels with E10 fuel due to its high oxygen content . This reduces air pollution , particularly in cities where there are many @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ industries . E10 fuel delivered through corn or sugarcane provides another market for farmers . This creates demand , which strengthens rural economies and employment in the agriculture industry . Using local crops reduces dependency on imported oil . <h> Drawbacks of E10 fuel <p> E10 fuel , for all of its benefits , comes with a few environmental downsides . One of those threats comes from the land use associated with ethanol . Growing crops for ethanol requires large swathes of farmland , which can contribute to deforestation and loss of biodiversity . When people expand their agricultural land at the expense of forests and grasslands , it can cause soil erosion and sedimentation . <p> Water use is also a huge problem . Ethanol production is water-intensive , which can worsen already serious issues in areas with water scarcity . Sustainable practices of water management are needed to mitigate these problems . <p> E10 fuel can also impact food prices . Diverting crops from food to fuel production can lead to higher prices for food due to the reduced supply for human consumption . Such a change can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ developing world , where access to cheap food is critical . <h> Performance and engine concerns <p> Ethanol blends can cause problems for some older cars ; they can be damaged when running on E10 fuel . Ethanol is corrosive to some materials used in older engines , which can lead to costly repairs . Before using E10 fuel , vehicle owners must first check the guidelines from vehicle manufacturers . Classic cars are particularly vulnerable to damage from E10 fuel . <p> Fuel efficiency is another consideration . There is no major problem with E10 fuel for the vast majority of modern cars , but it could slightly reduce your fuel economy since ethanol has a lower energy content per gallon than gasoline . However , E10 fuel does tend to be cheaper than regular petrol . <h> Balancing benefits and challenges <p> Using E10 fuel benefits the environment by reducing carbon emissions , but it can cause deforestation and damage incompatible vehicles . Investing money in research and development can create a way to make ethanol production more sustainable and efficient , and shape the future of E10 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ output , water consumption and commodity prices . Fostering innovation in agriculture helps reduce land use changes and conserve natural habitats . <h> Conclusion <p> There are several benefits and disadvantages of using E10 fuel . It holds immense promise both for climate change mitigation and agricultural livelihoods . That being said , land use , water usage and vehicle compatibility issues must also be addressed . <p> If you 're one of the people considering E10 fuel , this article has information that you should know about its effect on the environment and society . With wise buying decisions and a preference for the sustainable cycle , ethanol can deliver its virtues while mitigating its vices . However , finding that balance will be key for the future of E10 . The approach should consider environmental , economic and social factors , among other important aspects . <h> Save IA <p> It 's never been more important to help Independent Australia survive ! <p> Fearless news publication IA has exposed deep-rooted secrets other media routinely ignored . @@134765405 <p> Facing the devastating impacts of climate change , Pacific leaders are pushing to achieve 100% renewable energy in the next decade to act as a demonstration to other countries and regions as they fight for the survival of the countries and people . <p> But is this feasible ? <p> Some say the sweet spot for renewable energy is 80% , with each percentage point above that requiring a doubling in investment . <p> It 's also counter intuitive but getting to 100% renewable energy may also require investment in new diesel generators that have greater flexibility , dialling down or even switching off when renewable energy is abundant and otherwise providing assurance that standby capacity is available if needed . <p> It 's important that donors show flexibility in this regard , and avoid blanket bans on investment in fossil fuel generation such as the situation that prevents the use of gas to replace wood for clean cooking . <p> Before investing in new renewable energy assets , grid upgrades may also be required to support the two-way flow of electrons as consumer energy resources like solar PV @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ role in balancing supply and demand . <h> What are other jurisdictions doing ? <p> South Australia has shown that it is possible to get 100% renewable energy at times , including 100% solar PV and 100% wind energy , and has a goal to do that on average all the time by 2027 , up from 73% over the last 12 months , with the benefit of exports , imports and standby gas plants . <p> There are three key technologies to support 24/7 renewable electricity . <p> The first is big batteries which have evolved over the last eight years . Initially for frequency control and auxiliary services , then two-hours storage , followed by four hours and now eight hours are starting to emerge . <p> Some argue that with grid forming inverters , big batteries no longer need synchronous generation -- usually provided by fossil fuel -- to provide inertia , the beating heart of an electricity system . Also , consumer batteries can be networked as virtual power plants to achieve similar outcomes . <p> The second is smart meters which allow price signals for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to encourage use and increasing rates overnight or during periods of high demand and constrained supply to discourage electricity use . Smart meters also provide essential voltage information on the distribution network . <p> The third is demand response , typically industry but increasingly smart devices like air conditioners , electric vehicles , hot water systems or pool pumps which can be dialled down during periods of constrained supply . <h> But what about an island grid with no international connections to enable electricity imports and exports ? <p> Australian mine sites , offshore islands and remote communities are also showing that it is possible to achieve 100% renewable energy at times with the balance provided by gas or diesel . <p> Communities like the opal mining town of Coober Pedy now have an abundance of electricity , with an average of 70% renewable energy -- and fresh water from reverse osmosis -- provide an illustration of what can be achieved . <p> While possible , engineers currently say that there is a delta in battery costs that currently makes it uneconomic . <p> This could change in the future @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ relatively expensive lithium , nickel and cobalt with sodium or even vanadium flow batteries which have the advantages of long duration and are ideal to operate in exposed hot and salty environments . <p> There 's also another variable that comes into play -- batteries on wheels -- electric vehicles . With vehicle to grid technology now being deployed in Australia for select electric vehicles , electric vehicles can provide a key role in managing supply and demand in island electricity networks , charging when the sun is shining and discharging during evening peaks or even powering homes and businesses during disruptions to supply . <p> Similarly , charging infrastructure can be designed to support the grid , particularly with fast chargers backed by battery energy storage solutions that can also support the grid when required . <p> So the challenge is to design an energy system for the island that considers both electricity and transport and provides flexibility around pricing and demand response . <p> Thinking outside the box , what if renewable energy capacity was built to provide shore power for ships so they do n't need to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ other times this abundance of electricity could be used between visits , to charge batteries and create new business opportunities that could power down when ships are in dock . <p> So it is possible to get to 100% renewable energy , if not a little uneconomic until transport is electrified and the suite of smart devices is fully deployed . In the meantime , it is important to ensure the grid is flexible enough to incorporate renewable energy and demand management . <p> Barbara Elliston is a director of Elliston Power Consultants , Unison Networks , Easy Warm and the Smart Energy Council . @@134798002 <h> Interview : Jordan Giusti on Floodland , climate reckoning and the meaning of home <p> Lismore has long worn its floods as a badge of resilience -- a town that rebuilds , again and again , along the banks of a river that refuses to be tamed . But in Floodland , director Jordan Giusti looks beyond the mythology of grit and endurance to ask a far more unsettling question : what happens when resilience is n't enough ? <p> Set in what 's often described as Australia 's most flood-prone postcode , Floodland immerses us in the lives of Lismore residents navigating the aftermath of the catastrophic 2022 floods . But Giusti 's film is not simply a disaster chronicle . Shot in an intimate cin ? ma v ? rit ? style over several years , it captures the slow , complicated collision between history , climate change , politics , love and identity . We meet Eli , whose evolving love story unfolds against the uncertainty of repeated deluge ; we witness families reckoning with generational memory ; and we hear from First Nations voices , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's colonial past and its uneasy present . <p> Rather than delivering a conventional climate expos ? , Giusti allows the river -- and the people who live alongside it -- to speak . The result is a work that feels less like reportage and more like lived experience : immersive , human and quietly devastating . It 's a documentary that interrogates government response and policy failures , while never losing sight of the emotional stakes of home , belonging and survival . <p> Winner of the Sustainable Futures Award at the 2025 Sydney Film Festival -- the world 's largest environmental film prize -- Floodland announces Giusti as a filmmaker deeply attuned to both the political and the personal . By Anthony Carew . <h> The Testament of Ann Lee reaches for the divine <p> For anyone who 's ever had a three-day house party shut down by the cops due to noise complaints , does Ann Lee have a religion for you . <p> The founder of the 18th century Shaker movement , Lee built a church whose tenets rested on chastity , equality , dutiful labour ... and ecstatic worship that was wild , primal and very loud . Born in Mancunian squalor , she fashioned her faith from strains of revivalism and Methodism , before godly visions persuaded her -- and her followers -- that she was the second coming of Christ . <p> English orthodoxy was hostile to her teachings and the volume at which they were practised , so Lee eventually led her flock to the New World of the nascent American colony , where the Shakers found a more welcoming setting for freedom of religion , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ least , until she was inevitably accused of witchcraft . <p> A pin-up for piety and persecution , with her legend finding room for a few miracles , Lee is a figure worthy of sainthood and , in turn , cinematic hagiography . The Testament of Ann Lee , the third feature for Norwegian actor-turned-filmmaker Mona Fastvold , arrives with big-screen grandeur and a peerless headlining performance from Amanda Seyfried . It 's a fearless film in many ways , beginning from the daring conceit of taking its subject at her visionary word . <p> " How many stories have we seen about male icons on a grand scale , how many stories , again and again and again ? " Fastvold asked rhetorically upon her film 's Venice premiere . " Can we not get to see one story about a woman like this ? " <p> Fastvold fashions a portrait of a hero where another might render a villain . But The Testament of Ann Lee is ultimately all too speculative and strange to be a soft sell for the legacy of a little-known historical figure . A @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to depict the pursuit of transcendence , the film feels like the artistic opposite of the brand-managing biopics -- especially the musical ones -- that clog up streaming service menus and prestige picture slates . <p> Fastvold may have conceived her picture as a feminist rebalancing of the epic , but her film feels most like -- and works best as -- a sincere portrait of how music and dance are the ultimate expressions of the human desire for the divine . <p> On full release this week , The Testament of Ann Lee just served as the opening night film for Europa ! @@134801658 <p> It 's not easy to find silver linings amid the rapid , human-driven destabilization of Earth 's climate -- though that has n't stopped researchers from trying . One longstanding theory suggests that glacial melt could actually help slow climate change by feeding algae , but a new study just dumped cold water on the idea . <p> The findings , published in the journal Nature Communications Earth &amp; Environment , show that meltwater from an Antarctic ice shelf pumps far less iron into surrounding waters than scientists previously thought . The authors argue that this undermines the iron fertilization theory , which posits that iron-rich glacial meltwater would feed algal blooms that pull planet-warming carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere as they grow . <p> " Our claim in this paper is that the meltwater itself carries very little iron , and that most of the iron that it does carry comes from the grinding up and dissolving of bedrock into the liquid layer between the bedrock and the ice sheet , not from the ice that is driving sea level rise , " principal investigator Rob Sherrell @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a statement . <h> Field data challenges theory <p> Evidence to support the iron fertilization theory has primarily come from simulations and computer modeling . Sherrell and his colleagues wanted to test its legitimacy using real-world data , so they embarked on an expedition to the Amundsen Sea in West Antarctica . <p> The Amundsen has the highest rates of ice shelf thinning in Antarctica and therefore accounts for most of the sea level rise driven by Antarctic melting . When warm seawater rises up from the deep ocean and enters cavities beneath an ice shelf -- the seaward extension of a glacier away from the continent -- it melts the shelf from below , releasing freshwater into the sea . <p> At the Dotson Ice Shelf , the researchers collected water samples at the point where seawater enters one such cavity and the point where it exits after meltwater flows in . Study lead author Venkatesh Chinni , a postdoctoral researcher at Rutgers , then analyzed the samples in the lab to assess their iron content , while collaborators at Texas A&amp;M University measured isotopic ratios to pinpoint where @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that total meltwater only contributed about 10% of the outflowing dissolved iron , whereas 62% came from inflowing deep water . The researchers traced the remaining 28% back to inputs from shelf sediments . This contradicts the idea that meltwater could stimulate algal blooms enough to offset global warming . <h> The complexities of glacial melt and warming <p> While the study makes a compelling case against the iron fertilization theory , the authors note that a true understanding of the subglacial processes involved in iron flux requires additional research . <p> What 's more , they only investigated one Antarctic ice shelf , and the way water moves and mixes within subglacial cavities can vary depending on the shape of the shelf , nearby ocean conditions , and the properties of meltwater outflow . The researchers believe the fundamental balance of dissolved iron sources they observed at Dotson could generally apply to other ice shelves , but verifying this will also require further research . <p> This is n't the first study to question the iron fertilization theory . For example , previous research found that past spikes in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on carbon-capturing algae . Meanwhile , there is ampleevidence to suggest that glacial melt could exacerbate regional warming -- and therefore melting -- by darkening the surface of the glacier , causing it to absorb more solar radiation . <p> The interplay between the global climate and the marine processes that drive glacial melt is incredibly nuanced , which is why it 's so important for field studies to validate findings and theories based on modeling . Such work may not reveal many silver linings , but it will help scientists understand the future of a warming Antarctica .
