@@134837856 <p> A nightmare that has haunted generations of strategic thinkers and policymakers in Australia has come true : we live in a region increasingly dominated by an Asian great power . <p> China has rapidly become East Asia 's principal trade partner and strategic actor . If Australians want to be secure in the Indo-Pacific , we have no choice other than to recognise , if not embrace , this reality and the unforgiving logic of geography . <p> Even though China is famously Australia 's major trading partner , the rise of the People 's Republic is overwhelmingly seen as more of a strategic threat than an economic opportunity . True , Australia 's enviable living standards are potentially hostage to China 's increasingly assertive policy calculus , but its use of geoeconomic leverage is hardly unique . <p> This is understandably disorienting for political and strategic elites , especially at a time when the familiar architecture of the international order is being undermined by the United States , the country that has long been seen as its principal architect and foundation . With Donald Trump in the White @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ alliances are seen as potential sources of leverage . <p> It 's perhaps unsurprising , then , that supporters of the alliance and US primacy want critics to explain what a more productive relationship with China might look like and how it would fit with Australian values . <p> The hardest part of answering this question may be agreeing on what the greatest threat to Australia 's security actually is . I doubt anyone thinks a Chinese land invasion of Australia is likely . Even the much-discussed threat to our sea-lanes of communication seems a bit unlikely : why would the world 's largest trading nation want to disrupt the very system upon which its economic wellbeing depends ? <p> In such an environment , Australia 's possession of a handful of nuclear-powered submarines can make no difference to China 's strategic calculus : if China is not deterred by the United States , it 's not going to take much notice of anything we do . More to the point , even though history suggests it 's virtually guaranteed Australia would actively support the US in any possible conflict @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ US would return the favour . <p> Indeed , the US may even decide that maintaining a forward presence in our part of the Indo-Pacific is more trouble and expense than it 's worth . It 's not impossible that Trump may want to come to some mutually beneficial arrangement with Chinese President Xi Jinping , for whom the dealmaker-in-chief has expressed admiration . <p> A world of competing spheres of influence would be a very difficult one for Australia to navigate , especially if its primary allegiance were to a non-resident power . Under these circumstances , why not try to make the best of a bad job and construct a more productive relationship with China ? <p> An encouraging point about China is that it at least uses constructive language when talking about the sorts of issues we might hope to see addressed at this especially perilous historical moment . <p> ' A community of common destiny ' and an ' ecological civilisation ' do sound a bit unlikely , unless you think , as I do , that climate change is the single biggest challenge to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is that climate change is rapidly getting much worse and will continue to do so unless there are immediate , coordinated transnational efforts to do something about it . <p> It 's true that China is the biggest emitter of carbon dioxide in the world , but it 's also the biggest manufacturer and installer of solar power . Not only are China 's own emissions plateauing , but the cost of energy is coming down in places that desperately need it as a direct consequence of its efforts . This compares favourably with US climate policy . <p> I 'm not confident that even this will be enough to save us from much more serious environmental problems , but I am sure that if we do n't cooperate with countries that are at least trying to solve them , then fretting about Australian values will be the least of our worries . Significantly , even current and former military leaders recognise that climate change is becoming a major security problem . <p> I 've suggested elsewhere that Australia and China could set the world a good example by collaborating @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ could offer to cancel the new submarines if China stops building aircraft carriers , too . Arms control and increased spending on environmental remediation should be an unambiguously good idea at this point in history . Making them part of serious , open-ended national conversations about security would be welcome indeed . <p> Author <p> Mark Beeson is an adjunct professor at the University of Technology Sydney . Previously he was professor of international politics at the University of Western Australia , Murdoch University , and Birmingham University . 
@@134837860 <p> The judgment in the long-running greenwashing case brought against Australian gas producer Santos -- published earlier this week -- was , on its face , a blow to efforts to hold major fossil fuel companies accountable for climate change . <p> The Federal Court dismissed all greenwashing allegations levelled at Santos by the Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility ( ACCR ) , finding Santos had not misled consumers or shareholders about its decarbonisation plans or status as a producer of ' cleaner fuels ' . <p> The judgment was largely disappointing for those seeking to hold major fossil fuel producers , like Santos , accountable through legal action . However , analysis of the judgment provides useful insight into the status of Australian climate law and the extent to which the law continues to fail to grapple with the unique and complex issues of climate justice . <h> The allegations of greenwashing against Santos <p> The ACCR alleged that in a series of corporate reports published between 2020 and 2021 , Santos had made three key categories of misrepresentations that : <p> -- Santos is a producer of ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ energy ' . <p> -- Santos had a ' credible and clear ' plan , based upon reasonable assumptions , for reducing emissions in line with its 2030 and 2040 targets forming part of a ' Net Zero Roadmap ' . <p> -- Santos could , in the future , deliver ' zero-emissions ' or ' clean ' hydrogen , and hydrogen with ' no emissions in its production ' , while intending to produce ' blue hydrogen ' from fossil gas . <p> The case represented a first-of-its-kind legal test of the credibility of a fossil fuel company 's climate transition plans , particularly one that relies heavily on carbon capture and storage ( CCS ) technologies and carbon offsets . <p> Much of ACCR 's case centred on what it alleged were the unreasonable assumptions that Santos had made about its future business , including the future viability of CCS technologies , the size of the future market for hydrogen and the basis on which it claimed gas was a source of ' clean energy ' . <p> ACCR also alleged that Santos had made a series of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ concealed the impacts that its plans to increase the production of gas would have on the company 's future emissions and that Santos ' plan to achieve its emissions reduction targets was heavily reliant on the use of carbon offsets . <h> What is the law ? <p> While the term ' greenwashing ' does not appear in any corporate legislation , the act of greenwashing is effectively rendered unlawful by laws that protect against misleading or deceptive conduct or representations . <p> Various laws protect different groups from different types of misleading representations . For instance , the Australian Consumer Law is primarily focused on protecting the buyers of products or services from misleading claims and many of the provisions of the Corporations Act are designed to protect shareholders from misrepresentations about the prospects of the businesses in which they are invested . <p> In many cases , a key factor in determining whether a claim is misleading is a test of whether a person or company had ' reasonable grounds ' for making that claim . If someone does n't have ' reasonable grounds ' for a claim @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or deceptive . <p> The ' reasonable grounds ' test was considered throughout the ACCR v Santos judgment in assessing whether the gas company 's claims were misleading . Much of the court 's focus was on whether Santos had sufficient contemporaneous documentation of its decision making processes and the evidence it relied upon to make the statements it did . <h> What did the Federal Court conclude ? <p> In short , the Federal Court accepted virtually all of the counterarguments put forward by Santos and found that none of the issues raised by ACCR amounted to misleading or deceptive conduct . ACCR 's case was dismissed in its entirety , and ACCR was ordered to pay Santos ' legal costs . <h> Gas is clean and Santos is a clean fuels company <p> One of the more contentious conclusions of the Federal Court judgment is the acceptance of Santos ' claim that gas is a ' clean energy ' source and that the company is a ' clean fuel producer ' . <p> In finding those claims were not misleading , the court accepted that Santos had made @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' in comparison to other fossil fuels . The court found the ' statement does not convey that natural gas is " clean " but that it is in relative terms cleaner than coal and diesel . ' <p> The court concluded that a ' reasonable member of the target audience would have understood that consumption of natural gas was a material contributor of GHG emissions ' -- in other words , those reading Santos ' statements would have understood that Santos ' use of the term ' clean energy ' did not imply that gas produced zero emissions . <p> The court also found that Santos ' description of itself as a ' clean fuels company ' was not misleading , because Santos had the ambition of producing lower emissions fuels in the future : <p> ' the description by Santos of it as a " clean fuels company " was made in the context of its statements about the " transition to a lower-carbon future " and " the transition from natural gas to hydrogen . " That and the associated statement of Santos as a " clean @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ That is , as Santos put it , the type of company that Santos wanted to be as it transitioned to net zero by 2040. ' -- at 521 . <h> A Clear and Credible Plan to Net Zero <p> Santos ' corporate documents outlined what it described as a ' clear and credible roadmap ' for achieving net zero by 2040 , backed up by ' a realistic , doable plan ' and that it was a ' realistic roadmap , real activities and a plan to achieve net zero by 2040 . ' <p> This plan was largely predicated on Santos making significant progress in three key areas : being able to maintain its level of gas production while reducing emissions , expanding the use of carbon capture and storage technologies , and substantial growth in the market for net zero emissions hydrogen . It was also heavily reliant on the use of carbon offsets to meet targets . <p> ACCR alleged that Santos ' plan fell considerably short of being ' clear and credible ' , and that parts of the plan presented to shareholders were contradictory @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Crucially , the court held that despite calling it a ' clear and credible ' plan that was ' realistic and doable ' , that none of these statements amounted to a promise to actually deliver the plan . <p> ' The impugned statements concern Santos ' long-term objectives which necessarily and reasonably remained subject to uncertainty and contingencies and dependent upon the emergence of new markets . <p> The target audience would understand expressions like " realistic and doable " or " clear and credible " as measured descriptors setting expectations lower than certainty . That a plan is realistic suggests that it can be achieved but not that it will be achieved . ' -- at 828-829 . <h> CEOs and Senior Executives have singificant discretion <p> The fluid nature of Santos ' ' net zero roadmap ' was made clear in correspondence between senior Santos staff and its executives , and the manner by which the company produced forecasts of its future emissions and gas production . <p> While preparing a draft investor presentation outlining Santos ' net zero strategy , analysts within Santos produced a chart @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first version of this chart showed Santos ' future emissions rising in future years , corresponding to increases in forecast gas production . <p> This forecast was based on the analyst 's understanding of which projects Santos was likely to develop in the future , and the logical conclusion that increasing gas production would lead to higher company emissions . <p> But , when this chart was reviewed by Santos CEO Kevin Gallagher , changes were ordered . Emissions had to be flat , and so must gas production . <p> Draft Santos slide with handwritten comments from CEO Kevin Gallagher . Note the title ' Santos ' emissions increase to 2030 with production growth ' . <p> ACCR alleged that Santos had no reasonable grounds for assuming that both its emissions and gas production would remain flat out to 2035 . Evidence showed Santos ' internal teams were forecasting increases in both metrics and the ' flatline ' scenario that Santos ultimately published was purely based on the request from Gallagher . Internal correspondence showed that at least one analyst thought there was ' effectively no basis ' for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ruled that this did not mean the revised presentation was misleading or deceptive . Accepting Santos ' arguments , the court concluded that it is within the remit of CEOs and other senior executives to amend the findings of their own analysts . Stating at 643 : <p> ' Strategic decisions about production and emissions were made by the CEO and senior executives and not by more junior employees ... Unsurprisingly , intervening strategic decisions may need to be made after preparation of the data . That is what occurred in 2020 with the development of the Targets and the Net Zero Roadmap . ' <h> What does this mean for corporate accountability ? <p> On the surface , the case was a victory for Santos . Companies have significant flexibility when outlining their net zero targets and climate transition plans . Companies can consider the inherent uncertainty and evolving nature of future policies , markets and technologies as factoring into what constitutes ' reasonable grounds ' for those plans . <p> However , what the judgment really highlights is the extent to which ' the law ' is a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ delivering climate justice . <p> Part of the reason for this is that the fossil fuel industry actively works to prevent the emergence of new climate law . The fossil fuel industry knows it is on the wrong side of climate justice . It is in its ( short-term ) financial interest to maintain the legal status quo . <p> But the judgment reinforced factual findings that the use of fossil gas is a contributor to global emissions and worsening global warming . Santos ' representations might not be misleading , but that does not mean the company 's actions are an adequate response to the climate crisis that we face , and to which it is a major contributor . <p> The law will continue to evolve and the pressure on fossil fuel companies will continue to grow . <p> This article was originally published on Tempests and Terawatts . What I did not expect was the infrastructure behind the rhetoric . <p> Right now , Australian politics is unsettled . One Nation is polling at levels never seen before . The Coalition is scrambling for identity and leadership clarity . Electoral funding reforms will tighten disclosure laws and cap spending from mid 2026 , but much of the campaign structure built under looser rules remains intact . Third-party actors such as Advance -- and GetUp ! -- are no longer peripheral to our political ecosystem . Unemployment is much lower than it was a generation ago . There are millions more jobs . The minimum wage they are often paid is still one of the highest in the world . They have access to a universal health scheme . They are already accumulating superannuation savings for a retirement that will provide dignity . They will need it as they live longer and face a world restructured by artificial intelligence . Far more people are obtaining higher levels of education . @@134870105 <h> Albert Palazzo WA subs base the only reason for AUKUS <p> It is tempting to label the AUKUS project an exercise in self-delusion and self-denial . As if preparing for a let-down , a new report from the Congressional Research Service advances alternatives to the transfer of the promised submarines that will still allow the US to meet its strategic priorities . <p> In addition , it is hard to square the submarine promise with the reality that is Washington these days . The odds of the nation being able to increase its submarine build rate to the required level for the transfer to go ahead without a loss of US operational capability is virtually nil , according to a December 2025 report from the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies . <p> One must accept that Australia 's politicians are reasonably intelligent , yet with the myriad well-known problems facing the nuclear-powered submarine transfer it is hard to understand how they can still insist that the project is " full steam ahead " . How can our politicians sustain their faith in AUKUS and not be rightly labelled as delusional ? <p> The answer to this contradiction lies in recognising what AUKUS is really about -- what the parties actually expect to gain from the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in fact the most important part of the AUKUS deal -- they are a distraction . From the base , American submarines will be able to operate against China 's southern flank and sever its lines of communication across the Indian Ocean . @@134870111 <h> Red Stitch 's rare staging of all three plays in Ray Lawler 's classic trilogy illuminates the tragedy behind Summer of the Seventeenth Doll . By Robert Reid . <h> Red Stitch revives Ray Lawler 's The Doll Trilogy <p> In the canon of Australian plays , it 's hard to overstate the centrality of Ray Lawler 's Summer of the Seventeenth Doll . The Doll , as it is colloquially known , benefits not so much from any inherent genius in the writing -- the author would have been the first to eschew such a claim -- but rather appeared at a crucial turning point in the development of Australian theatre and national identity . <p> At the time of The Doll 's premiere in 1955 , at the height of the Menzies years , Australia was firmly in a period of imperial identification , but there was an emerging sense of maturing nationality . The transition from colonial-settler stereotypes of masculinity and class to those of an increasingly urbanised life caused a tension that The Doll captured with its depiction of the collapsing relationship between the itinerant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ captured the language of the time , the uncertainty underneath the brash nationalism of the ' 50s . The situational pathos he presents resembles the dark , epic storytelling of the corresponding golden age of American theatre . Like Louis Esson before him , Lawler portrays an Australia that exists in the suburbs rather than reproducing the mythic colonial outback . <p> Lawler returned to the play in 1974 , when he was commissioned to write two more plays about the characters by John Sumner 's Melbourne Theatre Company to celebrate the original 's 20th anniversary . This is when Kid Stakes and Other Times come into the picture , premiering at the Russell Street Theatre in Melbourne in 1975 and ' 76 respectively . Lawler continued redrafting his trilogy and in 1985 , Sydney Theatre Company presented the updated plays together as a cycle for the 30th anniversary . Red Stitch Actors ' Theatre presents this version , directed by Ella Caldwell , to mark their 25th anniversary year and the 71st anniversary of the plays . <p> I never thought I 'd see a production of all three @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ produced outside the trilogy , with close to 10 productions since its debut . Other Times has possibly had three standalone productions . Producing the whole trilogy is a major undertaking -- this may be only the third time . For anyone with any interest in Australian theatre , it 's a not-to-be-missed event . <p> The plays are not without their challenges to a contemporary audience . Lawler 's faithful representation of Australian street slang now requires an effort to understand , particularly in the prequels , in which the language is perhaps inevitably a stilted re-creation of language remembered from decades earlier -- unlike The Doll itself , which is set in the years when it was written and was urgent and immediate . <p> Kid Stakes and Other Times struggle under the weight of their forebear . Kid Stakes has the benefit of being an origin story and gains a lift from its narrative balance against the way we know the story ends . As its more frequent production demonstrates , it can stand alone . The couples fall in love , one of them has a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in how they react and the decisions they make . <p> Do you have to see the other two plays to understand The Doll ? No -- but if you do , you 'll understand what makes it a tragedy . <p> Other Times , on the other hand , is the difficult middle play and benefits most from the rewrites Lawler did over the years . The Red Stitch production is working with the 1980s edit , which is much cleaner and tighter than the 1970s production . It still suffers from a rhythmical lassitude that may be inherent in the postwar Melbourne setting . <p> It structures the trilogy as a kind of thesis about the effect of World War II on Australia . It 's worth noting that both Kid Stakes and Other Times were written in the shadow of the Vietnam War , and this edit allows Lawler to reflect on the impact of war generally through the lens of his own generation . I 'm not convinced it 's entirely successful as an argument , but it does reflect the trauma and anxiety of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be played by the same troupe of actors throughout , the cast is called upon to represent the four main characters in their late teens and early 20s , mid 20s and early 30s , and finally in their late 30s and early 40s . Only one actor , Khisraw Jones-Shukoor , plays a range of characters across the trilogy , filling the role of the outsider to the group . In Kid Stakes I sometimes found it hard to see through the age of the performers to recognise the characters ' ages , but by Other Times , hardened as they all are by the war , it ceased to be something I noticed . <p> Ngaire Dawn Fair plays an Olive who transforms from a giggling and impulsive teen , showing the gradually developing hard edges that make her the woman who can pick herself up after everything collapses and go back to work . Something about her performance reminds me of a young Genevi ? ve Picot . Ben Prendergast plays a Roo who has the traditionally taciturn exterior that betrays a sensitive heart -- a cypher @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inarticulate by the demands of patriarchy . <p> Caroline Lee presents an Emma ( Olive 's mother ) carved out of wood , formidable and indomitable , which makes her undoing within Other Times all the more wrenching . In a rapidly emerging post-liberal world order in which Australia 's place is far from certain , Olive 's optimism and disappointment feel both modern and antique . It was perhaps never necessary to see the story 's beginning to grasp @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ value of the prequels is in Nancy and Barney . An equally sized part still admired that a plant can be so persistent , so destructive of our attempts to shelter from the elements , to defy nature . <p> But , as I learnt , lichen is not a plant at all . Rather , it is the organism , or collection of organisms , for which the term " symbiosis " was first coined . <p> Lichen is a mix of fungus , algae and bacteria , none of which could exist in the same way on their own . A healthy lichen will produce chemicals that the component parts can not make when they are separated . It will change its form and colour depending on its location and component parts . <p> The bacteria -- cyanobacteria -- photosynthesise and also fix nitrogen -- something very few organisms can do . Cyanobacteria were the first organisms ever to produce oxygen . It was the cyanobacteria , over billions of years , that made our planet 's atmosphere . <p> Around the bacteria grow the filaments of fungus , making up its bulk and providing a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ off the nutrients created by the bacteria , and in turn anchors them and shelters them from the environment . <p> This composite beastie is the pioneer of the natural world . The thing that will bring down all our plans . <p> Lichen are the first organisms to colonise barren surfaces , such as my roof . Their filaments burrow into tiny cracks in those surfaces . They trap moisture and debris , and that , in time , becomes a home for other plants , insects and an entire ecology . <p> In time , lichen will destroy our structures . Bring them down . @@134897562 <p> I 've long been the archetypical swing voter .
